Food security: can drones and BeiDou put an end to ‘paper farming’ in China?
Expert calls for a change in approach after state media report alleged county officials misreported the size of rice fields to meet targets
The remarks came after a state media investigation alleged that officials in central China had inflated the size of mandatory rice crops to hit their targets.
CCTV programme Focus Report aired its investigation on July 14, claiming officials in Jianghua Yao – a county in Yongzhou, Hunan province – had misreported the extent of farmland used for growing rice.
It said officials claimed to have met their 2024 target by reporting 390,000 mu (26,000 hectares) of rice paddies had been planted in the county.
But the actual size of the paddy fields that year was far smaller at 238,000 mu (15,866 hectares), according to the report.
It labelled the practice “paper farming”, saying some of the crops existed only on paper.

Black Lake CEO’s strategy to sell AI solutions to factories: turn to food couriers
Tech company founder Zhou Yuxiang sits down with the South China Morning Post for his first interview with a Hong Kong media outlet
His entire sales team, hired from various industrial cities, survived a gruelling five-day boot camp on articulating how AI can solve specific manufacturing pain points.
“They are very street-smart,” the 36-year-old said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post. “Good college graduates are often thin-skinned. They linger in front of a factory and can’t get in.
“But for food delivery guys, they just give a cigarette to the security guard and get in … They can also bypass guard dogs, or find a back door to get into a factory to meet the owner because they deliver food.”
With a sales force of more than 420 delivery workers, Black Lake, established in 2016, has grown to serve 35,000 factory clients, 95 per cent of which are small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
The International Data Corporation also ranks it as mainland China’s top provider of cloud-based production management software.

full_text:
From fungus to fashion: Chinese scientists develop sustainable ‘living textiles’
The fabric can clean and repair itself, opening the door to recyclable fashion and biodegradable packaging
Chinese scientists have developed a way to create clothing and textiles from a fungus that can self-clean and regenerate.
The fabric can also be customised – for example to add colour or protect the wearer from ultraviolet (UV) rays – with the help of other microorganisms, according to a study published on Friday.
A persistent challenge for engineered living materials (ELMs) has been scaling up microscopic living cells into large, durable structures that remain alive and functional.
A research team led by the Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology tried to address this challenge by developing a method to make ELMs using a fungus called Cordyceps militaris.
Also known as caterpillar fungus, it is widely used in traditional Chinese medicine and can create threadlike structures.
The study highlighted the material’s sustainability. Environmental assessments confirmed it degraded within 41 days, raising the possibility the material could be used to make circular fashion – clothing that is designed to be reused or recycled.

A court has upheld the finding that Pauline Hanson engaged in racial discrimination against Mehreen Faruqi when she tweeted the Greens senator should “pack your bags and piss off back to Pakistan”.
The One Nation leader launched the appeal in November, almost a month after Justice Angus Stewart found Hanson engaged in “seriously offensive” and intimidating behaviour against Faruqi in the September 2022 social media post that breached the Racial Discrimination Act.
On Monday, Stewart’s decision was upheld by federal court justices Melissa Perry, Geoffrey Kennett, and Elizabeth Bennett.
Faruqi was in court for the judgment, but Hanson did not make an appearance.
Stewart had said the case had functioned as “a test case” for both Faruqi and Hanson’s claims. Faruqi wanted to prove a “common form of egregious behaviour is unlawful”, meanwhile Hanson wanted to prove in her failed bid that section 18C of the act breached the implied freedom of political communication.
Hanson had argued in her appeal that Stewart’s decision “raised alarm among many Australians that their freedom of speech, the freedom to say what they’re thinking, is constantly under threat”.
In November Faruqi described her win as a landmark decision and a “warning for people like Pauline Hanson”.
“I do hope it emboldens individuals and communities to assert their right to live free from racism,” Faruqi said.

title: ‘A new trajectory’: EVs now almost quarter of Australia’s new car sales as fuel crisis bites
summary:
More electric vehicles sold in first half of 2026 than whole of last year, new data shows

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australians bought more electric vehicles in the first six months of 2026 than the whole of the previous year, new data shows, as the ongoing crisis in the Middle East causes uncertainty about petrol prices.

There were 103,855 battery electric vehicles (EVs) sold nationally between January and June, compared with 103,269 in 2025, according to data from VFacts and the Electric Vehicle Council.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Australians bought more electric vehicles in the first six months of 2026 than the whole of the previous year, new data shows, as the ongoing crisis in the Middle East causes uncertainty about petrol prices.
There were 103,855 battery electric vehicles (EVs) sold nationally between January and June, compared with 103,269 in 2025, according to data from VFacts and the Electric Vehicle Council.
Battery EVs as a share of new car sales doubled compared with the same time last year, making up 23.4% of sales in June 2026 compared with 10.3% in June 2025.
Sales of plug-in hybrids were also outpacing last year’s figures, with 54,121 sold in the first six months of 2026 compared with 53,249 throughout 2025. Plug-in hybrids made up 11.5% of all sales last month, compared with 4.8% in June 2025.
Julie Delvecchio, chief executive of the Electric Vehicle Council, said the sharp rise was driven by unique circumstances. “It’s clear that the fuel crisis has reminded all of us how reliant we really are on overseas fuel.”
As a result, she said, EVs as “something that people may have been considering jumped to the top of the list”.
“We’re hopeful that it will be a sustained trend, but we’ll have to wait and see,” she said. “What we do know for sure is that once people switch to an EV, they generally never go back.”
Fuel prices were expected to rise again after the government’s temporary cut to the excise ends this coming Sunday.
Diesel prices are up by about 50 cents in July to about $2.20 a litre in the major east coast cities.
George Whitcombe, an EV analyst at Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, whose data revealed similar results, said it was rare for an automotive market to experience such a significant increase in EV sales. “This sets that market on a new trajectory.”
In addition to elevated fuel prices and uncertainty as a result of the conflict in Iran, Australia’s EV growth is also being driven by legislative changes under the federal government’s vehicle efficiency standard, Whitcombe said.
However, national uptake is still behind other countries, he said. “Many European markets now have penetration rates [the proportion of people in a market likely to buy a product] above 30%, with penetration rates in the Nordic countries now above 50% and as high as 92% in Norway.”
Tony Weber, chief executive of the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries, said the increase signalled EVs were moving beyond the early-adopter market and becoming an increasingly significant part of Australia’s broader new vehicle market.
The sales spike in recent months could reflect a combination of new-model launches, vehicle availability and concerns about fuel prices, he said. He noted that in 2026, 80% of EV sales occurred in two of 20 market segments: small SUV and medium SUV.
“The ongoing transition will depend on vehicles remaining affordable and the continued expansion of model choice into new market segments, providing a viable choice for consumers.”

title: AusAlert test: what time will national emergency warning siren sound on phones in Australia today? Here’s what to know
summary:
National emergency test alert will be sent to all compatible mobile devices on 27 July, with domestic violence advocates advising how to turn off safe phones

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Virtually every phone in the country will blare an emergency siren at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July as part of the first Australia-wide test of a new national warning system called AusAlert.

Most phones, and some smartwatches and tablets, will receive a pop-up notification and an alert sound that cannot be silenced – even if your device is on “do not disturb” or silent mode.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Virtually every phone in the country will blare an emergency siren at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July as part of the first Australia-wide test of a new national warning system called AusAlert.
Most phones, and some smartwatches and tablets, will receive a pop-up notification and an alert sound that cannot be silenced – even if your device is on “do not disturb” or silent mode.
What is AusAlert? AusAlert is Australia’s new national warning system, which will send emergency messages to mobile devices during local and widespread disasters.
Authorities currently use SMS texts to alert people about safety information. The new system will instead send a mass broadcast via mobile phone towers, with an alert popping up on devices, similar to a phone notification.
It will launch nationally in October, months after the national alert test.
What will happen during the national test? “On Monday 27 July 2026, a test alert will be sent to all mobile devices in Australia. This includes most phones, and some smart watches and tablets,” the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) advises.
Users will hear a siren and see a pop-up notification on their phone, which will look different depending on the device, but with text including “TEST MESSAGE” and “NO ACTION IS REQUIRED”.
Video of the AusAlert test “What people should expect to hear is a siren that will last for about 10 seconds,” said Pat Hetherington, the interim coordinator general at Nema.
He said it would be “loud enough to get people’s attention” but quieter than a fire alarm.
“It will be noticeable, but it won’t won’t be too over the top.”
What time is the AusAlert test around Australia? There have been local tests, but Monday will be the first nationwide test, occurring at 2pm AEST, which is:
 
  2pm for New South Wales, Victoria, the ACT, Queensland and Tasmania.
 
 
  1.30pm in the Northern Territory and South Australia.
 
 
  12pm in Western Australia.
 
 Why is the AusAlert emergency warning system test needed? Hetherington said AusAlert came from a recommendation of the royal commission into the 2019-20 black summer bushfires, which called for a nationally consistent warning system.
“The existing system is based on standard SMS capability, and throughout a series of emergencies and disasters, that system has had real latency in terms of people receiving the messages,” he said.
“You [could] get network congestion, text messages may not come through in a timely way … or come through at all, dependent upon who your provider is.”
Kristy McBain, the federal emergency management minister whose electorate of Eden-Monaro was hit by the black summer bushfires, said some people in her area didn’t receive emergency text alerts during that disaster because their phone provider was unavailable.
The new system allows nationwide alerts as well as localised “geofenced” alerts such as for floods or even warnings to boil water in emergency situations.
The emergency services minister, Kristy McBain, says the AusAlert is ‘far superior’ to current warning systems.  Photograph: James Ross/AAPMcBain said AusAlert was a “far superior” system and would reach “more people in a more timely manner” than current warning systems used by state governments. Existing systems will still be used in future, with McBain describing AusAlert as “another tool in the toolkit”.
Will every phone ring or make a sound during the alert test at 2pm AEST? Essentially, yes. Hetherington said phones made after 2019 should receive the alert, but some older phones may not.
The alert will come through on all compatible devices even if you are on a call, or if the phone is on silent. Nema has advice that about 80% of Apple iPhones will ring, and some 16m Android devices.
“The only way to not receive a critical alert is to turn your mobile device off or switch it to ‘airplane mode’,” Nema advised.
The agency said the alert will go to:
 
  iPhone models 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later.
 
 
  Apple Watch models SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later.
 
 
  Android devices running Android 12 or later.
 
 Older Androids, or those not using iOS or Android “might still receive AusAlerts”, Nema said, but Apple iPads will not.
Hetherington and Nema’s deputy coordinator general, Katarina Carroll, said the agency had engaged with “thousands” of groups including schools, businesses and even funeral associations to warn of the alert test.
They said it was important to run the test during an “ordinary” time of day so people knew what to expect in future.
But noting some people may find it inconvenient to have a loud siren ring alert, such as during an important meeting or a funeral, Hetherington and Carroll said “if you have your phone off an hour before and an hour after [2pm AEST], we’re confident you won’t receive that message”.
Other countries around the world have had problems in testing or using such systems, with alerts delayed or not arriving at all. Nema said it had “learned a lot” from tests around the world and it was well prepared for Monday.
What about ‘safe phones’ for those experiencing domestic and family violence? Domestic and family violence advocates have raised concerns about the risk of the alert exposing “safe phones”, or devices kept hidden for safety reasons by those experiencing violence.
Nema said the agency had engaged with family violence experts about the test, including assisting advocates to disseminate safety information, and posting a safety guide on its website .
Hetherington said phones switched off or on airplane mode would not receive the alert, and said: “The message for safe phones and hidden phones is very much [to switch off for] a 24-hour period.”
Carroll added: “The advice is if there’s anything that’s happening [during the test], have it off for an hour or so. But certainly for domestic and family violence, there’s that broader advice for that extension of time [24 hours].”
Groups such as the Women’s Safety Commissioner, DV Connect and the Council of Single Mothers and their Children have issued safety advisories to this effect.
What do I have to do when I receive the AusAlert? Nothing at all. The test requires no action.
However, Hetherington encouraged Australians to answer a survey or give feedback after the test to help Nema assess the success of the trial and any changes that may be needed.
“People should read the message. But it is a test that doesn’t require people to do anything,” he said.
“We’re obviously interested in hearing if people haven’t received the message.”
When will AusAlert be used for real? Nema suggests the warnings could be used for legitimate hazards such as bushfires, floods, cyclones and earthquakes; serious public safety issues or terrorism; biosecurity incidents; and major public health incidents.
States and territories will be able to send alerts.
“I would expect some states to use it quite a lot, particularly where you want information to get out almost in real time,” Hetherington said.

title: House of the Dragon Just Unceremoniously Killed Off a Main Character. It Was the Right Move
summary: And his death was as unceremonious as they come
full_text:
Warning: This story contains spoilers for Episode 6 of House of the Dragon Season 3.
After two seasons of cementing himself as one of the most hated characters in Westeros history (which, as Game of Thrones fans know, has no shortage of reprehensible monsters), Ser Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel) ultimately went out with little more than a whimper in Episode 6 of House of the Dragon Season 3.
Following his declaration in Episode 5 that he intended to die a warrior's death by leading his men on a suicide mission into the path of Team Black's massive army of Rivermen and Winter Wolves, Cole was erased from the board within the first 10 minutes of Sunday's installment. The episode opened with Cole and his remaining Greens falling into a trap set by young Lord Oscar Tully (Archie Barnes) and Lord Roderick Dustin (Tommy Flanagan) that saw a host of Rivermen play dead in order to lure their enemy into battle. Although Cole's forces triumphed in the scuffle, they soon realized the real trick was that they were surrounded by the full strength of the Black army.
Cole attempted to bargain for his men's lives by promising surrender and, when that offer was refused, put forth a bid to decide the battle by facing Oscar and Roderick in two vs. one combat. But Team Black obviously had no plans of letting Cole go out in the blaze of glory he so greatly desired. Without waiting for either lord to even deign to respond, archer Alysanne Blackwood (Annie Shapero) let loose three arrows that struck Cole down, unceremoniously killing him. Their army then advanced on his men to slaughter them.
Those who have read George R. R. Martin's Fire & Blood will recognize this event as the massacre known as the Butcher's Ball. And in the book, it's made abundantly clear Team Black meant for Cole to die as undignified a death as possible. As one Riverlands knight bluntly remarks to Cole's dead body, "I'll have no songs about how brave you died, Kingmaker."
In House of the Dragon, it was ironically Cole himself who set the scene for his anticlimactic demise—because really, how often does a character in the Thrones universe actually get what they want? "I am the realm's greatest warrior," he told Ser Gwayne (Freddie Fox) in Episode 5. "And I will die as such. Clear-eyed. Unbent. Glorious in battle. And not in their service, finally. But in my own. And they will sing songs of it. And Queen Alicent herself will hear them."
Despite proving himself to be the Dance of the Dragons' most hypocritical player, by shifting his allegiance to Alicent (Olivia Cooke) and the Greens back in Season 1, Cole managed to convince himself he was walking the path of righteousness. No matter how deplorable his actions were, in his mind, everything he did was to uphold honor, duty, and the law. But after witnessing the devastating power of dragonfire firsthand at the Battle of Rook's Rest in Season 2, Cole's view of the conflict began to spiral into nihilism. In the end, the only way he felt he could leave his mark on the world was to go down swinging in battle.
"Criston Cole started as a soldier before the 20-year stretch that he spent at King’s Landing—that’s how he started, and that’s how he wants to finish," Frankel told Variety of his character's motivations in Season 3. "In his mind, the only honest version of himself is the soldier. Everything else is pretense; the diplomat is pretense; the Hand of the King, there’s a level of pretense; Lord Commander of the Kingsguard, there’s a level of pretense. I suppose they’re all psychological, brain-led jobs. He isn’t that way, he’s very much led by his sword and his fighting instinct. The idea that that’s how he will be remembered, I think, feels honest."
But Cole doesn't get the poetic, honorable last stand he thinks he deserves, reinforcing the futility of common soldiers fighting a war of nobles and stripping him of the fantasy of a worthy legacy in his final moments. Seems like Alicent will never hear those songs, after all.

title: Crypto is the canary in the coal mine for the quantum computing threat, experts say
full_text:
Crypto is the canary in the coal mine for the quantum computing threat, experts say
As estimates for “Q-Day” move closer, experts warn that crypto’s slow governance, not its cryptography, may be the biggest obstacle to defending against quantum attacks.
- Quantum computing could first expose vulnerabilities in crypto networks, positioning Bitcoin as an early warning system for broader financial infrastructure risk.
- The real bottleneck is governance, not cryptography, as Bitcoin’s slow, consensus-driven upgrade process lags behind centralized institutions.
- “Q-Day” is a gradual threat, not a single moment, with attackers needing only enough quantum power to break encryption before assets lose value.
Quantum computing is a risk factor for every encrypted system on the planet, including major banks. But crypto, due to the way it works, may be the technology that gets tested first.
"Cryptocurrencies are the canary in the coal mine," Eddy Zervigon, CEO of Quantum Xchange, said in an interview with CoinDesk. Zervigon's firm builds infrastructure to shield networks, including financial ones, from quantum-enabled attacks, and he's blunt about where the first casualty is likely to show up.
"That's the first place of attack because of the decentralized nature," Zervigon said. "Once you see it happening there, then you know that someone somewhere has a cryptographically relevant quantum computer."
A cryptographically relevant quantum computer, capable of breaking the elliptic-curve cryptography underpinning the Bitcoin blockchain's signatures, along with the encryption securing bank rails, doesn't exist yet. The consensus estimate for when it will is compressing, not stretching.
"The folks spending billions of dollars, like Microsoft, IBM, and others developing quantum computers, generally believe there will be a commercially relevant, cryptographically relevant quantum computer in the 2029 timeframe," Zervigon said. "That's not me making stuff up. That's based on what people like Arvind Krishna at IBM have said."
That estimate is consistent with recent hardware developments. Earlier this year, Google researchers revealed that breaking the elliptic-curve cryptography safeguarding top cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ether would require fewer than 500,000 physical qubits, a 20-fold decline from previous estimates. That prompted several observers, including Google, to pull forward the so-called Q-Day deadline to 2029.
The White House, meanwhile, is aiming to develop a powerful quantum computer by 2028 and shift high-value assets and federal data to post-quantum cryptography by 2030. "That sets the clock. It creates a sense of urgency,” Zervigon said.
Consensus speed is the real risk factor
Zervigon isn't alone in pointing to slow governance, not cryptography, as crypto's weak point.
Deutsche Digital Assets framed it as a clear cut speed differential between TradFi and decentralized rails.
"The difference — and this is the honest answer to the 'Bitcoin is uniquely vulnerable' narrative — is governance speed," the bank wrote on July 23.
It explained that an investment bank like JPMorgan does not need to get a go ahead from millions of pseudonymous global participants before upgrading its cryptographic infrastructure.
“It needs a board resolution, a budget, and a vendor. Large financial institutions can and will migrate to post-quantum standards faster, more quietly, and more predictably than a decentralised public blockchain. That is not an argument against Bitcoin. It is an argument for taking its governance process seriously,” Deutsche Digital Assets added.
Academic literature, such as the 2024 arXiv paper "Downtime Required for Bitcoin Quantum-Safety" validates this argument citing Bitcoin's own upgrade history as the cautionary precedent.
"Before any upgrade process can be commenced, a 90% consensus among Bitcoin miners has to be achieved over the particular details of the upgrade," the researchers wrote. "Historically, considerable changes to the Bitcoin network have been met with high resistance. A notable example of this was the SegWit upgrade in 2017."
That upgrade triggered disagreement in the community to such an extent that the Bitcoin blockchain eventually split into several different versions through hard forks, creating the Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin Gold networks.
The takeaway, therefore, is that post-quantum cryptography itself could be ready in time. What's uncertain is whether Bitcoin's governance layer can arrive at a 90% consensus to deploy the defenses.
Q-Day isn't a print, it's a trend
Markets tend to model this as a binary event, where encryption holds until a specific date, then it doesn't. Zervigon says that framework is wrong, and it understates how early the risk actually bites.
"Everybody talks about the moment you can break an algorithm," he said. "You don't necessarily need to do it in one moment to be effective. If it takes me three months or six months to decrypt data that still has value, I've achieved the same goal."
That collapses the usual timeline math. A quantum computer doesn't need enough throughput to break a signature in real time to be a threat, it only needs enough throughput to get there before the underlying data or funds stop being worth stealing.

title: Triple-A confirms treasury-wallet breach after losses reach $11.8M
summary: The stablecoin payments company said client funds were unaffected and that the financial impact would be absorbed through its treasury reserves.
full_text:
Triple-A confirms treasury-wallet breach after losses reach $11.8M
The stablecoin payments company said client funds were unaffected and that the financial impact would be absorbed through its treasury reserves.
Stablecoin payments firm Triple-A confirmed that unauthorized access to its treasury wallets resulted in the loss of company-owned digital assets.
On Monday, the Singapore-based company said it detected the unauthorized access on Saturday and temporarily placed certain services into maintenance mode for about three hours while it secured the affected infrastructure. Triple-A said client funds were not affected because it does not custody digital assets on behalf of customers and keeps client funds separately in trust accounts with safeguarding institutions.
Triple-A did not disclose the amount lost or explain how the wallets were compromised. Onchain investigator Specter previously estimated the losses at about $11.8 million.
The company said the financial impact was limited to specific operational accounts and would be absorbed through its treasury reserves. It added that all services had been restored and transactions and settlements were processing normally.
Triple-A said it was working with cybersecurity specialists, blockchain forensics firms and authorities, including the Singapore Police Force, to investigate the incident, trace the assets and support recovery efforts.

title: South Korea’s KB Kookmin Bank to launch cross-border payment service on JPMorgan’s Kinexys: report
summary: The largest bank in South Korea plans to launch a blockchain-based cross-border corporate payments service next month, according to Yonhap.
full_text:
South Korea's KB Kookmin Bank to launch cross-border payment service on JPMorgan's Kinexys: report
Quick Take
- KB Kookmin Bank, the largest bank in South Korea, plans to launch a blockchain-based cross-border corporate payments service next month, according to Yonhap.
- The bank is set to roll out the service under a partnership with Kinexys by J.P. Morgan.
We'd love your feedback.
KB Kookmin Bank, the largest bank in South Korea, plans to launch a blockchain-based cross-border corporate payments service using Kinexys by J.P. Morgan, according to local media reports.
Yonhap News Agency reported Sunday that the bank is set to roll out the service next month under a partnership with Kinexys. It will become the first Korean financial institution to use Kinexys' blockchain payment network for corporate import and export settlements, per the report.
The service will be available through the bank's domestic branches in South Korea and its Singapore branch. Initially, the bank plans to prioritize U.S. dollar transfers across 10 countries: South Korea, the U.S., Singapore, Saudi Arabia, India, Thailand, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain and South Africa, according to the report.
KB Kookmin has been expanding its presence in blockchain-based payments. In March, KB Kookmin Card, one of the country's largest credit card companies, announced that it is building a hybrid stablecoin payment model with Avalanche.
Kinexys is J.P. Morgan's blockchain business unit that enables programmable payments, asset tokenization, and near-real-time settlement for institutional clients.
Meanwhile, NHN KCP, a South Korean payment service provider, also signed a memorandum of understanding in April with Ava Labs to develop a payments-focused Layer 1 network.

title: Does Yamaha’s silent violin really work?
summary: Plus blenders, hairdryers and lawnmowers that do the job quietly
full_text:
Does Yamaha’s silent violin really work?
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Soft play
“Every day, [mankind] invents machines and gadgets that multiply noise and distract [us] from essential life, from reflection, from spiritual immersion,” wrote the dadaist sculptor Jean Arp more than 80 years ago. He would have been even more troubled by the cacophony of the 21st century. Nevertheless, a more tranquil trend is emerging in consumer electronics. That is partly down to Quiet Mark, an organisation associated with the Noise Abatement Society, which conducts acoustic tests on the level and quality of sound made by products, then certifies the best performers in each category.
Founder and CEO Poppy Szkiler notes that when Quiet Mark started, little thought was given to the noise levels of consumer products, but in recent years – particularly post-pandemic – companies have been innovating rapidly. Musical instruments are, of course, designed to make sound, but practice sessions can cause friction with family, flatmates and neighbours. Yamaha’s Silent range – which now includes piano, guitar, brass and stringed instruments – debuted more than 30 years ago in Japan, where the dense urban environments made it immediately popular. While not strictly silent, these instruments vastly reduce the acoustic volume produced, with headphones picking up the slack.
I’m not a violinist, so I enlisted professional fiddler Jennymay Logan to accompany me to Yamaha Music London to try the SV250 and its five-string sister, the SV255. A cable runs from the instrument to a small control box, which has volume, treble and bass controls along with outputs to headphones (or an amplifier). On the back of the instrument is a knob to balance between the two pick-ups, one on the bridge, the other within the body, such as it is (the absence of the traditional violin body is one of the instrument’s most distinguishing features, while having an external control box also makes it lighter). The amplified sound was superb, the body pick-up contributing a rich, sonorous tone, and the bridge pick-up emphasising higher frequencies. The sound in the room? No louder than a wasp on a window pane.
Smooth operator
The sound of ice cubes being crushed by a metal blade is never going to be harmonious, but Quiet Mark rates Magimix’s blenders as some of the least noisy on the market. That’s partly down to the industrial-grade induction motors that the French firm uses across its range, and partly the heft of the build; this unit, complete with a borosilicate glass jug, weighs more than 5kg. Does it blend hot soups and milkshakes to a smooth consistency? Certainly. And can you be heard over the top of it without shouting? Yes. The premium model, costing £100 extra, adds two blend cups for smoothies on the go and a mill attachment for grinding spices or making small quantities – for baby food, for example.
Express yourself
Breast pumps were part of the parenting routine in our home for a time, and our experience was similar to the one described by Sarah O’Leary, CEO of Willow, which owns the Elvie brand. “Traditional breast pumps are loud, they disrupt your life,” she says. “There was clearly a very fundamental, unmet need for women who were breastfeeding, and a big factor in designing the Elvie Pump was recognising the trauma of that experience.” A great deal quieter, slimmer and more discreet than the machines I remember, these are powered by a small, coin-sized piezo pump, and can be linked to Elvie’s app to help keep track of sessions during sleep-deprived periods.
Low blow
Founder of Mdlondon Michael Douglas envisaged the Blow as a quieter hairdryer that would let stylists talk to clients. My four-year-old son was helpful during testing; he hates the noise made by hairdryers and hand dryers and immediately runs away when they start up. But he was untroubled by this one, whose sound is more of a higher-pitched whoosh than a standard hairdryer blast. That seems consistent with its compact size and weight – just 360g – but my wife (who, unlike me, has hair) reports that it’s more powerful than her usual dryer. It comes with diffuser and concentrator attachments, three speed and heat settings and a cool-shot button to create styles that stick.
Cut through the noise
Unlike lawnmowers of old, the A 6v from Stiga’s new robot range is guaranteed not to shatter the calm of a Sunday, rolling about silently and cutting grass at a volume comparable to an electric shaver. Unable to hear it working while indoors, I popped outside to check on its progress and found two cats watching it, unperturbed. It’s not the smoothest of set-ups (a few attempts to upgrade firmware were needed via the Stiga app), and the initial mapping has to be done using an on-screen joystick (slightly fiddly), but after a couple of edits all was set. There’s flawless navigation via quad-band GPS, with a camera to help it avoid obstacles and return to the charging station.

title: NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC
summary: The prime minister says he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.
full_text:
NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC
- Published
Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.
In his first major interview since becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.
The prime minister also suggested making it harder to claim benefits, saying the country had to get serious about getting the welfare bill down.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has meanwhile written to the prime minister, saying he should rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to fund social care reform.
Burnham told the BBC that if the government did not reform social care, the NHS would "collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not needed to end up in the NHS system".
But pressed on whether he would create a new system before the next election, he said he "couldn't put a timeline on it right here, right now", though he would put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care".
Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown, and a year later pursued the idea of a compulsory levy to fund it.
One of the options floated by that Labour government was allowing people to defer the payment until after they died, which led to the Tories branding it a "death tax".
Burnham is due to make a speech on adult social care on Wednesday.
The BBC understands the PM will stop short of unveiling plans for a new system in this speech, instead announcing he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review that has been considering possible solutions for social care.
Baroness Louise Casey is not expected to give her final recommendations until 2028, but Burnham wants to bring her schedule forward.
He told the BBC: "Social care was on a longer path and I have brought it straight forward."
Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home with tasks like washing and cleaning.
Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.
In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.
Sarah Woolnough, chief executive of healthcare think tank the King's Fund, said the current "punitive system" meant that "quite a lot of people go without care that they need", with one in seven paying in excess of £100,000 for social care.
While Burnham has not yet outlined any plans, Woolnough told the BBC Radio 4's Today programme that reforms could range from making social care free at the point of need to placing a cap on the amount people spend.
"The PM has for a long time mooted the idea of a social care system similar to NHS," she said.
"It would be expensive but on the scale of what we spend on other public services - around £200bn on the NHS - we are talking for some of these options low billions per year."
Adult social care has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.
Two years ago Sir Keir Starmer was criticised when Labour scrapped plans for an £86,000 cap on the amount people in England would spend on social care in their lifetime.
Badenoch wrote in her letter to Burnham that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".
Layla Moran, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the Health and Social Committee, warned against the issue becoming a "political football".
"We do need to discuss where the money is going to come from but also we need to all be putting our political capital into this," she told the Today programme.
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said he was ready to do "whatever I can to find a real and lasting consensus on social care".
He said: "Family carers must be at the heart of any new system, everyone must get the care they need and no one should lose their home as a result."
Reform Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said social care needed fixing but warned the party would fight any proposal for a "universal death tax".
He said: "It's not fair to raid people's life savings and drags hundreds of thousands more families into paying tax when their loved ones pass away."
Andy Burnham: the Laura Kuenssberg Interview
What kind of prime minister will Andy Burnham be? Laura Kuenssberg has been behind the scenes with him during his first week in power.
Benefits reform
The prime minister also addressed the issue of benefits in his interview.
He said he might "increase the conditions on people required to receive benefits", telling the BBC he believed "there are people out there who, with the right support, can go into work."
He added: "It's about changing the nature of the support and making some of the support conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them. So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits. "
He said he would not go "straight to blaming " people on benefits, saying "there are people in the benefits system, young people in their 20s who have been quite seriously let down because the support wasn't there for them when it should have been there".
In the wide-ranging interview, the prime minister also spoke about how he would be prepared to call out Donald Trump to defend Britain's national interest.
On a lighter note, Burnham was asked if his dog Axel would be moving in to Number 10 Downing Street.
He said "Axel would have to stay up north" because he would not get on with Larry the Cat.
He said Axel, who is part bichon frise, part poodle, has "got that angry little man thing going on" and "I don't think the nation would thank me if I brought Axel down to disturb Larry's world", joking ,"these are the big decisions. The big decisions they've been made."

title: Behind-the-scenes at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM
summary: Laura Kuenssberg was given unprecedented access to the new prime minister’s first days in power.
full_text:
"You can clap now," a Downing Street official with a clipboard instructed the staff eagerly lining the halls of No 10 in the moments before the new prime minister walked in.
The applause duly began before the famous door opened, so the first sight and sound to greet Andy Burnham and his wife were crowds of clapping staff, crammed into the Downing Street hall. They stretched up the long corridor all the way to the door of the Cabinet Room - left ajar for him to walk straight in and get down to work.
I've seen plenty of prime ministers come and go from outside No 10. But I'd never been allowed inside at that moment before, able to hover outside the Cabinet Room and grab a quick word with the country's new leader at such an intense, symbolic time.
I have rarely seen a politician look as thoroughly delighted as Burnham, pride bursting out of his buttoned-up suit - that's right, the T-shirt and bomber jacket didn't make it to No 10 - or a leader who has wanted to stop and shake as many hands.
Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview
Panorama
What kind of prime minister will Andy Burnham be? In his first major broadcast interview since taking office, Laura Kuenssberg asks about his plans - and the challenges ahead.
No 10 staff are already wondering if they'll ever be able to stick to a regular prime minister's schedule, normally designed with military precision. If Andy Burnham was able to take the time to stop and speak to everyone in the country, I suspect he probably would.
It's a sign of his different style that our team was given permission to be behind the scenes at three key moments in the 59th prime minister's first week in charge - when he became Labour leader, when he walked into No 10, and on day one at his new Manchester outpost, No 10 North.
Most important by far was our half-hour interview in that shiny new office, after weeks during which Burnham was chased by accusations he'd avoided tough questions. But the extra glimpses we were given, alongside Burnham's own voracious appetite for social media, display a prime minister that's not just at ease in front of the cameras, but a leader who wants to bring you along for the ride.
They included revealing moments that are normally hidden - his first steps into the Cabinet Room to appoint his team, rating pub snacks with his Chancellor, John Healey, in an Instagram post, external, and sharing pictures with us of the family dog, Axel, whom he describes as having "angry little man energy".
"Comms" - how politicians communicate and explain themselves and talk to the public - is not the be-all and end-all.
Burnham's exploits online have already brought mockery and launched a thousand memes. But if a leader can't get your attention to make their arguments - as Keir Starmer found so challenging - ultimately, they are not going to get very far at all.
And the biggest difference of the Labour reboot so far is how the government looks and sounds. They've put an obvious priority on punter-friendly announcements such as cutting VAT from energy bills and tax breaks for pubs - although it is important to note the details on how to pay for all of that are not yet clear.
For Burnham though, telling his story is the easy part. Joking about the unique stink that accompanies Scampi Fries, or showing me his gold disc on loan from The Smiths' guitarist Johnny Marr, won't help him deal with US President Donald Trump, find money for defence, or create a new service to care for the elderly and vulnerable in England. Nor will it be any use as he grapples with the country's huge debts, changing demographics or public concerns about immigration.
Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.
Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.
But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.
Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".
When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024.
But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?
And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.
What about welfare? Remember Sir Keir ditched most significant reforms in the face of resistance on the back benches. While seeking not to "blame" anyone receiving benefits, Burnham said the country had to "get serious" about getting the welfare bill down, and suggested he might make it harder for some people to claim, by imposing extra conditions.
He didn't want to give much away about where he was going to find extra billions for defence, or pay for public services. He repeated that he'd stick to the promises on income tax, VAT and National Insurance made in 2024. But the prime minister clearly pointed to a possible shake-up of the council tax system, where those with the most expensive properties might have to pay considerably more. Changes like that to council tax, or to welfare, would be huge political moves that would put him on a collision course with some of his party, and some political opponents too.
Then, when it comes to matters of war and peace, which for Burnham are genuinely new, it felt we could see him thinking in real time how to answer the question, perhaps trying to balance giving a flavour of who he is, without creating a political accident.
Does he trust Trump? Twice he wouldn't say.
"It's a changing world," his second answer.
Would he take a call from Russian President, Vladimir Putin?
A pause, then: "I'd have to know the circumstances".
As mayor, Burnham evidently spent years thinking hard about how to use power, and how he wants to shift the balance in the UK away from Westminster. The impact of that stance could be profound, way beyond some admirably shiny No 10 signs emblazoned all over one floor of a government building in Manchester.
Mayors are expected to get power to spend nationally collected income tax, and crucially to spend billions without strings.
Burnham spent time too as mayor absorbing people's experiences, their hardships and frustrations.
"My strength always is in remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change because I am prime minister," Burnham told me.
Although don't be in any doubt, he also spent time thinking and planning about how to make a return to the political heart of this country, the Westminster he believes is so flawed.
But when it comes to the gravest matters that prime ministers have to deal with - security, power around the world, or the country's long-term economic stability, we're perhaps yet to see if Burnham's ambition for No 10 is accompanied by truly new big ideas that match the scale of his rhet

title: Funeral boss who lied about burying dad has shown no remorse, daughter says
summary: Robert Bush is being sentenced later for a string of offences, including denying proper burials.
full_text:
Funeral boss who lied about burying dad has shown no remorse, victim says
- Published
A woman whose dead father was discovered at an undertaker's three months after his funeral says her hellish ordeal has "crucified" her.
The body of Peter Moody, 65, was found by police alongside 34 others and more than 100 sets of ashes at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024. One of the bodies had been there for a year.
Former funeral director Robert Bush, 48, of Otley, West Yorkshire, will appear at Hull Crown Court later for sentencing. He previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.
Peter Moody's daughter Joanne Moody, 48, who is expected to join other families wronged by Bush in the court's public gallery, said: "It's broke me, it's crucified me. He has shown no remorse. No sympathy."
In addition to preventing lawful and decent burials, Bush, 48, previously pleaded guilty to 35 counts of fraud by false representation and another of fraudulently running a business, relating to the sale of funeral plans.
He also admitted one count of theft, which related to money stolen from collections meant for 12 charities, including the Salvation Army and Macmillan Cancer Support as well as local causes.
In a move that provoked anguish among affected families, Bush was granted conditional bail after entering his final guilty pleas in April.
But Moody said she would "sleep easier" knowing he would pay for his crimes.
"It's a pivotal point in our recovery knowing that justice is being done," she said.
Moody said she could now "start remembering dad as he was, not thinking about Bush walking the streets".
"I can't cry any more," she added.
She described her father as a "dedicated" family man who enjoyed fishing, Hull FC and spending time with his grandchildren.
Moody said Bush's guilty pleas had brought her some peace of mind.
"My dad was a person, he was not just a number or a statistic," she said.
"Now I can talk about him as the former dock worker who loved nothing more than standing on King George Dock and watching the ferries go out."
Prior to establishing Legacy, Bush worked for a number of other funeral directors. He oversaw more than 2,000 funerals during his career.
Many former customers said Bush had presented as the archetypal, caring undertaker; a point noted by Hull West and Haltemprice MP Emma Hardy.
"He tried to act like he cared, like he was their friend," said Hardy, who supported many of the families.
She said Bush had "exploited the most vulnerable people" when they were at their lowest ebb.
In June 2024, after Bush was exposed, Peter Moody's family held a second funeral for him - six months after the first.
His daughter described the first, including how Bush had "rushed us out" of the service, leaving the family "unable to grieve together".
"As soon as the curtains were closed on my dad, he wanted us out," she added.
'Licence to print money'
Charities have also been left reeling from Bush's offending.
He stole the collection held at the funeral of a former Hull trawlerman.
The money was meant for the Hull Fishing Heritage Centre, a charity that supports the city's former trawlermen and their families.
Chairman Jerry Thompson said: "I do not know how he [Bush] can sleep at night."
He said Bush had effectively turned his position into "a licence to print money".
Meanwhile, Moody said she would never recover.
"I still have his [her father's] number in my mobile and I can't bear to delete it," she said.
"He was always only a phone call away and I miss him so much."

title: Three dead and several injured in shooting at food festival near Seattle's Space Needle
summary: Several others, including a two-year-old boy, were also injured. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson says a suspect is in custody.
full_text:
Three dead and several injured in shooting at food festival near Seattle's Space Needle
- Published
Three people have been killed and several others injured following a shooting at a food festival near the Space Needle in Seattle on Sunday, the city fire department said.
Mayor Katie Wilson said one suspect was taken into custody following the incident at the Seattle Centre, which had been hosting the annual Bite of Seattle food festival across the weekend when the shots were fired at around 18:00 local time.
A second suspect fled the scene and is yet to be apprehended, assistant chief of Seattle Police Tyrone Davis added. He said it is believed the suspects were shooting at each other.
Two deaths were confirmed at the scene, with one person dying later in hospital. Those injured include a two-year-old boy, officials said.
Videos shared online showed people taking shelter inside the city's iconic Space Needle.
People could be seen crouched on the ground, taking cover behind pillars and shelves of merchandise in the Space Needle's lobby during the shooting.
The Seattle Police Department said an investigation remains ongoing and urged the public to avoid the area.
Wilson said in a statement that she wanted to "thank the Seattle police officers who responded to the scene and took a suspect into custody".
She had originally announced two suspects had been taken into custody before updating her statement later on Sunday evening.
Four of the injured were taken to hospital in a stable condition, while a fifth chose not to, the fire department said.
Representatives for Seattle and Washington state have condemned the shooting as an act of "senseless violence".
"My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe," Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said on social media.
Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, who represents Seattle, added: "Our hearts go out to all those impacted by this senseless violence," she wrote on social media.
"We are in close touch with Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and Governor Bob Ferguson, and co-ordinating across multiple levels of government to get updates on the situation."
Wilson also condemned the shooting as an "act of horrific violence".
"Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection, and joy ended in gunfire."
"Tonight, our attention belongs to the people whose lives were taken, those fighting to recover, and the families beside them," she added.
"Seattle grieves with you, and we will stand with you in the difficult days ahead."

title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
summary: The education minister's resignation, a rare setback for the Modi government, brings hope to many young protesters that their voices will be heard.
full_text:
'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
- Published
In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct.
So education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on Saturday, after more than a week of intense street protests, became a defining moment - one many young people celebrated as a rare victory.
In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests".
Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit.
Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years".
On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times.
Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram."
The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal.
The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families.
Initially, the protest drew little attention. That changed on 18 July when Delhi police forcibly removed and hospitalised hunger-striking educator Sonam Wangchuk.
Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them.
The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country.
Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed.
Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning".
"For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says.
Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage.
Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded.
"Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says.
Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture.
India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data.
Even graduates are struggling: a 2026 Azim Premji University study found fewer than 7% of jobseekers secured permanent salaried work within a year, and fewer than 4% landed white-collar jobs.
The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year.
On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended.
"I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices."
Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over."
A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next".
But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension.
Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees".
But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations.
Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40.
Human Rights Watch says, external that under Modi, Indian authorities have "routinely prosecuted activists, journalists, and peaceful protesters on fabricated counterterrorism and hate speech laws".
Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual".
At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".

title: Man and woman die after being pulled from sea off Cornish beach
summary: A man and a woman both died at the scene after being recovered from the sea.
full_text:
Man and woman die after being pulled from sea
- Published
A man and a woman have died after getting into trouble in the sea off a popular beach.
The two people were pulled from the water off Fistral Beach in Newquay, Cornwall, at about 21:45 BST on Sunday, about 15 minutes after HM Coastguard said it was called.
Devon and Cornwall Police said both were both confirmed dead at the scene.
Search and rescue teams from Newquay, Padstow and St Agnes took part in the operation, along with lifeboats from Newquay RNLI and a coastguard helicopter.
The force said their families had been informed and a file would be prepared for the coroner.
"Our thoughts are with them at this extremely difficult time," the police added.

title: Rapper Yung Filly tells trial 'vibes were good' with woman who accuses him of rape
summary: The rapper takes the witness stand at his trial in Australia where he denies raping a fan in a hotel room.
full_text:
Rapper Yung Filly tells trial 'vibes were good' with woman who accuses him of rape
- Published
UK rapper Yung Filly has told a court that the "vibes were good" between him and a woman he is accused of raping after performing at a nightclub in Australia in 2024.
The rapper, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, took the witness stand at the District Court of Western Australia on Monday - a week after the start of his trial.
He is accused of sexually assaulting the woman, then 20 years old, in his hotel room after he performed in Hillarys, a coastal suburb of Perth.
Barrientos, 30, has pleaded not guilty to six counts of sexual penetration without consent, three counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, and one count of strangulation.
Barrientos told the court he had "fancied" the woman when they met at the concert venue. He had been in the VIP area while she leaned over the barrier from the general area.
He denied touching her inappropriately.
"I recall putting my hand on her waist," he told the court. But he said he had not put his hands down her pants or touched her breast.
The "vibes were good" between them later when they arrived at his hotel, Barrientos said.
His security guard took the woman's phone away - a "standard practice" to protect their privacy, according to Barrientos.
The court heard previously that the pair had engaged in consensual sex before Barrientos turned violent and she told him to stop.
Barrientos, who had been touring Australia at the time of the alleged offences, is also known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad, and has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.
He has been on bail since being charged and was allowed to fly home to the UK in September for four months, before returning to Western Australia ahead of his trial.
In addition to his 1.8 million YouTube subscribers, he has three million followers on TikTok and and 2.4 million on Instagram.

title: Infantino tells Fifa critics to 'meditate, pray or watch football'
summary: Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about him and the World Cup.
full_text:
Infantino tells Fifa critics to 'meditate, pray or watch football'
- Published
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has told critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership, the governing body and the World Cup.
In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account - reposted to Fifa's eight million followers - Infantino addressed "those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens" to affirm his belief that, while they were "busy planting seeds of hate", Fifa was delivering the "greatest event on earth".
He said the World Cup "celebrated humanity at its best", adding that the 2026 tournament had "100% safety and security, only joy and happiness".
Infantino downplayed several of the tournament's high-profile controversies and hailed the involvement of Iran, who featured at the World Cup despite their ongoing conflict with co-hosts the United States, as a success.
He said Fifa "worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war", with Iran entering the country "without incident or conflict".
His comments are in stark contradiction to those of Iran's head coach Amir Ghalenoei, who said his team were the "most oppressed" at the World Cup.
- Infantino's 'time is up' with Fifa - La Liga boss - Published5 days ago
 
- The country that doesn't play football... yet - Published6 days ago
 
Iran faced visa delays, "integral" members of their backroom staff were denied entry to the US and fans had their allocation of tickets revoked, while Iran also had to move their training base from Tucson, Arizona to Tijuana, Mexico following a multitude of logistical issues in the build up to the tournament.
They later also encountered restrictions on their movements as they travelled between their training base and group matches in Los Angeles and Seattle.
Such issues were not unique to Iran, with fans from Haiti, Senegal, and Ivory Coast impacted by travel bans imposed by the Trump administration, while Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry to the US - despite holding a diplomatic passport and a single entry US visa - because of his "association with suspected members of terror organisations".
Infantino wrote: "You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world. Because football unites the world, and it was impressively demonstrated this summer."
Doubling down on the tournament's safety, Infantino said there were "zero incidents, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness".
However, Fifa is investigating Argentina's actions after players and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain's players after losing the World Cup final. It is also investigating allegations of racist abuse towards American social media influencer IShowSpeed, while supporters were arrested at multiple matches - including following England's semi-final against Argentina in Atlanta.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were also controversially present at World Cup stadiums.
Infantino also addressed criticism surrounding the standard of officiating at the tournament, in particular concerns about political interference after USA forward Folarin Balogun was made available for their last-16 tie when his one-match ban was suspended by Fifa - following the intervention of US President Donald Trump.
Of the 191 other red cards shown at a men's World Cup, only one other player has escaped a suspension.
Uefa said the decision had "crossed a red line", labelling it "unprecedented, incomprehensible, and unjustifiable", while the Norwegian Football Federation is considering filing a formal complaint to Fifa's ethics committee.
Infantino, however, argued that such decisions are not out of the ordinary, claiming similar rulings are "routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide".
He added: "It's curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising."
The International Olympic Committee has said it will not investigate Infantino for any possible breaches of political neutrality, stating the complaint levelled by human rights campaign group FairSquare falls outside the jurisdiction of its ethics commission.
Infantino's advice to his opponents was "to show some love" and "respect" to a tournament where "people came together as families, as fans, as one".
"To everyone who missed our beautiful game, the emotions, the celebrations, the laughter, the crying, the deception and the joy. To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents and parents come together for the beautiful game... sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," Infantino wrote.
"While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate. Our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning.
"To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions.
"Because only our beautiful game can deliver such an extraordinary show, a show where everyone becomes one and reconnects as humans.
"I am incredibly proud, as Fifa President, to have contributed, even a little, to this show. It's a great feeling."

title: Diomande agrees Real Madrid terms as PSG step away
summary: RB Leipzig winger Yan Diomande agrees personal terms with Real Madrid after Paris St-Germain withdraw their interest.
full_text:
Diomande agrees Real Madrid terms as PSG step away
- Published
RB Leipzig winger Yan Diomande has agreed personal terms with Real Madrid after Paris St-Germain withdrew their interest.
The 19-year-old Ivory Coast international was previously a target for Liverpool, who had an initial bid of £69m rejected in June, as well as PSG.
Liverpool then moved on to other targets, and PSG have now opted against entering a bidding war with Real.
PSG are said to have had a final £102.5m bid rejected for the teenager on Sunday.
Madrid have since agreed personal terms, said to be modelled on England midfielder Jude Bellingham's contract as they are incentivised on performances and effectively improve year-on-year.
Real will pay more than £100m for Diomande, who joined Leipzig from Spanish club Leganes last summer on a five-year deal.
- 'Everything I do is for you' - how tragedy is driving Diomande - Published20 June
 
Sources close to Real say key negotiators Jose Angel and Juni Calafat have been scouting Diomande for about five years, but were not reactive to Diomande's World Cup performances.
Leipzig have tried hard to keep the forward in Germany but regard the interest in Diomande as extraordinary, so have found it difficult to reject the interest - and potential record sale price - from Europe's elite clubs.
Diomande was the Bundesliga's young player of the season for 2025-26, having scored 12 goals and registered eight assists last term.
He moved from his native Ivory Coast to an academy in the United States in 2025 before joining Spanish side Leganes.

title: Tadej Pogacar wins Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time
summary: The Tour triumph marks the Slovenian's third win in a row and draws him level with four others on the all-time list
full_text:
Tadej Pogacar wins Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time
The Tour triumph marks the Slovenian’s third win in a row and draws him level with four others on the all-time list
Slovenia’s Tadej Pogacar secured a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title on Sunday after safely navigating the final stage, won by Mathieu van der Poel, to seal a third consecutive crown in cycling’s greatest race.
The 27-year-old UAE Team Emirates XRGcyclist, affectionately known as “Pogi”, only needed to avoid a race-ending mishap on the run into Paris to join Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain as a five-time Tour champion.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3India win second T20 in Zimbabwe to take series as Kishan and Varma shine
- list 3 of 3F1 needs better balance between business and sport, says Norris
Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel finished second overall, while Mexico’s Isaac del Toro rounded out the overall podium in third.
“Thank you to all the fans and to all of France for hosting this great race,” Pogacar said.
“Thank you to my competitors for putting on a great show. We fought hard over the last three weeks.”
Van der Poel takes final stage
Pogacar and Van der Poel broke away on the final ascent of Montmartre with about 10km (6 miles) remaining and took a slender advantage into the run to the Champs-Elysees as the chasing group closed relentlessly.
The Slovenian’s challenge faded inside the final kilometre, but Van der Poel pressed on to secure victory in a photo finish ahead of Alpecin-Premier Tech teammate Jasper Philipsen, with Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek in third.
“When I was sick last year, and I had to watch the stage on television, I was already thinking about this moment,” Van der Poel, 31, said.
“The way it went, it’s a dream. It’s incredible. It was super hard, and to be up there with the best rider in the world, all my respect for Tadej.
“I thought we were going to get caught back, then I was just thinking about this moment. I put my head down in the last 500 metres. I just went as hard as I could.
“I’m super happy. I have a few races I still wanted to win in my career, and this was one of them.”
Supreme Pogacar
Pogacar underlined his supremacy throughout the Tour by claiming five stage victories.
His path to a third straight yellow jersey became less complicated when two-time Tour winner Jonas Vingegaard, widely regarded as his principal challenger, withdrew after a crash on Stage 15.
The Tour’s traditional finale in Paris was shortened after security forces were redeployed to help tackle wildfires near Bordeaux. As a result, Stage 21, which customarily takes the peloton into Paris before several laps of the Champs-Elysees, was reduced to 89km from the 133km originally scheduled.
This year’s race also produced a remarkable first: no rider from France, Italy or Spain won a stage, making it the first Tour de France without a stage victory from any of the three nations that created and host cycling’s Grand Tours.
Pogacar’s latest triumph caps three weeks of racing since the Grand Depart in Barcelona and further cements his status as the dominant rider of his generation.
