Loading...
The Memphis Safe Task Force does not release a breakdown of its arrests. A dashboard maintained by the city, which has gotten pushback from the community for its lack of detail and transparency, had immigration arrests listed for the first few weeks, but those numbers disappeared.
Much of the task force's operations have been focused on traffic stops, and the immigration arrests seem to have happened largely during those, according to activists and constitutional observers.
"That's been the main way that families have been separated," says Oceja, of Vecindarios 901, noting that in the first few months, law enforcement was "pulling people over left and right."
She says the hotline was getting so many calls reporting traffic stops on well-traveled routes that they eventually set up a Facebook channel where people could receive alerts on the safest ways to go.
"We weren't sleeping," she remembers. "It was a very, very traumatic time for our community."
Hunter Demster, a Memphis resident who films as much task force activity as he can, says the traffic stops seem to be centered in the two main Hispanic neighborhoods in the city.
"It was very evident that this was an immigration operation at its core," he says. "This isn't necessarily about finding the worst of the worst or fixing crime. It's about targeting Black and brown folk."
Community leaders say the shock the task force brought was immediate and far-reaching, mirroring scenes from places like Minneapolis and Chicago during the height of immigration raids, as people were afraid to leave their homes for fear of being detained.
"There was a spike of fear and panic," says Mauricio Calvo, president and CEO of Latino Memphis. "Kids were not going to school, people were not showing up to work. We were getting calls from medical providers saying people were not coming in."

title: Baltimore will turn 911 into more than just an emergency number
summary: Baltimore is rethinking what it means to call 911, and who responds. Callers who don't need police will get help finding social services and healthcare before they actually fall into crisis.
full_text:
Baltimore will turn 911 into more than just an emergency number
Baltimore to overhaul how it responds to calls for mental health and other services
In March in a McDonald's parking lot off a busy Baltimore street, mental health clinician Michala Williams met a 38-year-old woman in a car.
"So, you called the police for help?" Williams asked the woman, who was sobbing uncontrollably and said she sometimes thinks about harming herself.
She told Williams she has children ranging from age 2 to 22, she was dealing with health issues, and that her fiancé had recently been jailed. She felt so overwhelmed she couldn't eat.
The woman, who asked not to be named so that she could freely discuss her mental health, explained she'd tried to get help the previous month by driving to the hospital but got pulled over on the way because her car registration had expired.
"I don't care if I get pulled over," she said. "But I was saying, 'I don't know what to do. I just want to go to the hospital.'"
The officer arrested her for acting erratically, so instead of going to the hospital she went to jail.
"I had to sit inside of a cold cell. I couldn't use the bathroom or anything," the woman said.
On the day she met Williams, she'd decided to call 911. The dispatcher recognized the woman didn't need a police response but instead needed one of Baltimore's mobile crisis teams, which send a clinician and a peer counselor to meet people in mental health distress.
By the end of an hourlong conversation, Williams set the woman up with referrals to a psychiatrist, a therapist, legal help, and a case manager to determine if her child with autism was eligible for government services.
"She's been through a lot of trauma, and no one is going to deny that," Williams said. "But I now have to take all of that and decide, 'OK, here's steps 1, 2, and 3,' because we got to find a little bit of sliver of something to give her some hope that there's help out here."
Problem solving 24/7, without badges, guns or handcuffs
For years, the mobile crisis teams, which are overseen by Behavioral Health System Baltimore, a nonprofit that acts as the city's mental health department, have diverted calls from police to mental health professionals. However, the units have a limited scope, focused on people in mental health crises.
Now Baltimore is tapping into some of the roughly $400 million it has received from opioid-related legal settlements to build out a broader service to operate around the clock and respond to other kinds of crises when police aren't needed.
Baltimore logged 1.68 million calls to 911 in 2024, but tens of thousands of them didn't require traditional emergency services, like police, firefighters, or EMTs, according to Tahir Duckett, an expert in community safety at Georgetown Law.
Instead, the calls were about, for example, a homeless person who fell asleep in a store, a person who seemed confused in a public park, and someone who was yelling at passersby on the street.
Such calls "don't require a badge, a gun, and handcuffs to resolve," Duckett said.
Often those people end up in jail instead of getting the help they need, he said.
A study recently found that when a non-law enforcement team responded to 911 calls in Durham, North Carolina, it resulted in fewer arrests than when police responded — especially for callers who were Black, men, or ages 25-39.
Police responses can also lead to trauma for that person or a less satisfactory outcome than another community service response would produce, Duckett said.
The idea behind the Baltimore mobile crisis teams — and the new service — is to find out what people in crisis may need and how to connect them to those resources instead of arresting them.
How a legal windfall will pay for expanded 911
From 2021 to 2025, Baltimore's homicide rate decreased by 60%, setting records for the drop in violence. But at the same time, drug overdoses made national records, as about 1,000 people here died of an overdose each year from 2020 to 2023.
In 2018, Baltimore opted out of a global settlement that other jurisdictions made with opioid makers and distributors and instead sued them independently.
As these opioid-related lawsuits settled, city officials decided that the settlement awards it receives must be spent on drug-related harms — or on services that help prevent addiction such as housing support, healthcare, and education.
One new program seeks to directly address overdoses by placing boxes of the overdose reversal drug naloxone at every subway stop.
Expanding 911 services is part of a larger strategy to beef up city services, with $15 million in settlement funds allocated so far, according to Sara Whaley, Baltimore's director of overdose response.
Whaley hopes the expansion will help the city think differently about how it responds to residents in crisis — regardless of why they're calling 911.
She views the calls as an opportunity to help solve a problem rather than be punitive. "What are the wraparound services and support that can help prevent them from being involved in this, in that emergency system?" she said.
For example, the person falling asleep in a store may need connection to community housing. The goal is to reduce violence, get people proper resources, and avoid the cycle of incarcerating people dealing with poverty, addiction, and mental health.
'The right response at the right time'
Rebecca Neusteter, executive director of the Health Lab at the University of Chicago, studies the impacts of services like these. She said they offer peace of mind for callers that "they're going to be met with the right response at the right time."
"We also see responders themselves feeling like they have a better toolbox in their ability to pursue actual resolution to these calls," she said.
To expand its system, Baltimore looked to cities — including Durham — that have adopted similar models to reroute callers who don't need emergency responders.
Durham's diversion program is called the Holistic Empathetic Assistance Response Team, or HEART. The program estimates it has diverted more than 12,000 calls in four years. It said police backup was needed for only 0.02% of those calls and that response times have improved for all types of 911 calls.
Durham has collected descriptions of the HEART calls, showing that nonpolice responders in Durham have helped with everything from finding housing for a woman fleeing domestic violence to setting up medical appointments for a homeless veteran.
In one case, a hotel manager called 911 asking for help finding a blind man housing for the night, since the hotel didn't have accessible rooms available. The HEART responders booked him a room and the next day provided a ride to meet with an organization that could help secure housing.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WYPR and KFF Health News.

title: Kalshi attacks a Wisconsin law banning election bets as 'voter suppression'
summary: The spat between the leading prediction market company and a key battleground state could be a glimpse into the next major fight between states and the fast-growing industry.
full_text:
Kalshi attacks a Wisconsin law banning election bets as 'voter suppression'
Ann Jacobs is a commissioner with the Wisconsin Elections Commission, a quiet, low-profile state agency that oversees elections. Recently, though, her day was anything but quiet.
"I was sitting at my desk, and all of a sudden Twitter was showing a lot of alerts," said Jacobs, who watched a flood of posts inundate her screen from employees, lawyers and other boosters of the prediction market company Kalshi.
"My reaction was, boy howdy are they mad," Jacobs said.
The outrage took Jacobs aback because of what set off the attacks: a commission advisory informing voters that they cannot place a bet in an election in which they cast a ballot.
Wagering on such a race could disqualify a ballot, or even result in a referral to state prosecutors, according to the commission's statement.
This is not a new policy. The advisory was simply stating the basics of a Wisconsin election law originally passed in 1849, Jacobs said.
"You can't be a felon on active supervision and vote. If you're 17, you can't vote, and betting on an election where you vote, it's the same thing, it's not allowed," she said.
Jump ahead to 2026, and Kalshi, the company leading the prediction market craze, is criticizing the law, calling it "bananas," "illegal" and a type of "voter suppression."
Watching employees of the multibillion-dollar company whip up a social media frenzy against an antebellum Wisconsin law left Jacobs puzzled.
To her, pointing out election law months before an election was "simply responsible work by a government entity."
The commission was spurred to issue the warning as prediction markets have become increasingly mainstream and a more prominent part of political discussions.
"We want people voting for the person they think will do the best job at the position they are being elected to. We don't want people voting for someone who isn't the best person for the job simply because it is going to line a voter's pocket," Jacobs said.
Election expert: Betting raises election integrity concerns
Billions of dollars are traded every week on prediction market sites Kalshi and Polymarket.
Nearly half the states, including Wisconsin, are locked in legal battles with Kalshi over who should regulate prediction markets. States insist the companies are no different than gambling operators and should be subject to state gaming laws, whereas Kalshi and the Trump administration say the federal government should oversee prediction markets as a financial product known as "a swap."
As the legal fights bang on, the bets keep pouring in.
Big sporting events, like the NBA finals and the World Cup, saw tens of billions of dollars wagered. The companies expect the midterm elections to be another massive event.
Yet that vision conflicts with another reality: Election betting is illegal in some or all circumstances in 32 states, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
"There should be absolutely no money involved in the outcome of our democracy. We should be voting on candidates for their positions and policies to represent us, not because we can make a buck," said Matt Barreto, director of the UCLA Voting Rights Project.
Election betting presents numerous possible election integrity issues, he said.
Foreign actors or partisan interests could use prediction markets to make a candidate appear more popular than they are in an effort to influence turnout.
Then there's the potential for insider trading, something that has dogged the prediction market industry, where everyone from President Trump's teleprompter operator to a special forces soldier has been accused of trading with confidential information. Kalshi has said it blocked "dozens" of political campaign staffers who have tried to bet on their own candidates since May.
Imagine, Barreto said, how this could play out during the midterms.
Say a poll worker places a bet on one candidate, and in order to make money, the person slows down the vote count or does an intentional undercount to change the real election result.
"If we found people who were somehow connected to either political campaigns or to the administration of elections, in the secretary of state's office or county elections office, were somehow involved in this, in the same way that Pete Rose tarnished the sanctity of baseball," said Barreto, referring to the baseball legend who was banned from the sport in 1989 in a betting scandal.
Charles Stewart, who runs MIT's Election Data and Science Lab, said most states have vote-counting checks that would prevent such manipulation from happening, but it is a hypothetical that could become part of already heated political discourse.
"If you are looking for a reason to be skeptical about election results, election officials trying to manipulate them for financial gain becomes another straw to grasp at," Stewart said. " However, these people don't need prediction markets to concoct some conspiracy theory to explain away why their candidate lost."
Kalshi declined to comment.
The company has argued that election betting will engage people who might not have cared otherwise about politics. The company argues that states like Wisconsin trying to prevent election betting are engaged in "voter suppression," because some voters who place wagers on a race might also be motivated to vote in the election — when they otherwise might not go to the polls.
Barreto does not buy that argument.
"If they sincerely cared about voter suppression, they would use some of their profits to set up a charity to mobilize the vote," he said.
Kalshi is not backing turn-out-the-vote efforts.
The company did recently launch something else: a midterm election dashboard to allow traders to monitor and place money on dozens of races at once.

Mass protest may have put Taipei mayor Wayne Chiang in pole position to contest the island’s next leadership election
The unexpectedly large turnout on Saturday appears to have given the island’s main opposition party, the Kuomintang, fresh momentum ahead of the local elections in November, and could reshape the race to become the party’s candidate in the next leadership election in 2028.
The demonstration outside the office of Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te was the largest opposition rally since Lai came to power two years ago.
Protesters accused the government of mishandling a scandal involving soybean salad oil found to contain excessive levels of the carcinogen benzo[a]pyrene, demanding that Lai apologise and Premier Cho Jung-tai resign.
It showed that food safety could mobilise people in a way that cut across party lines, according to Chang Yuan-hsiang, a political-science professor at Soochow University in Taipei.

title: Beijing fires new salvo at Tokyo with documentary on disputed Diaoyu Islands
summary:
Beijing is stepping up its global messaging campaign over East China Sea islets that Tokyo also claims by rolling out a five-part documentary to tell its version of history.
The state broadcaster’s English-language channel, China Global Television Network (CGTN), released the first part of Diaoyu Dao: Small Islands, Big Stakes on Monday to “examine the history, legal debates and contemporary realities” surrounding the group of small, uninhabited islands, which Japan administers as the...
full_text:
Beijing fires new salvo at Tokyo with documentary on disputed Diaoyu Islands
Series comes as political and maritime tensions have been ramping up between the neighbours for months
The state broadcaster’s English-language channel, China Global Television Network (CGTN), released the first part of Diaoyu Dao: Small Islands, Big Stakes on Monday to “examine the history, legal debates and contemporary realities” surrounding the group of small, uninhabited islands, which Japan administers as the Senkakus.
Historical texts and maps showed that the islands were first discovered, named and used by China before being ceded to Japan under the 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki following the first Sino-Japanese war, according to the series.
Beijing maintains that Tokyo was obliged to return the islands under the 1943 Cairo Declaration and the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation, two international documents that laid the foundation of the post-World War II global order.
Tokyo rejects the claim that historical maps have any bearing on the islands’ sovereignty. It asserts that China did not control the islands before 1895 and that the islands were not covered by the Treaty of Shimonoseki. It also cites the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty and the 1971 Okinawa Reversion Agreement with the United States to uphold its claim.
“Some scholars argue that key legal questions arising from these agreements remain unresolved,” the preview of the CGTN documentary said.

full_text:
A baby is missing off the coast of South Australia after the bodies of a mother and her toddler were pulled from the ocean.
Emergency services were called to the state’s southernmost coastal town, Port Macdonnell, at about 11.15am on Monday after a car was found with its engine running.
Officers launched a search and found two bodies in the ocean a short time later.
They have been identified as a 36-year-old woman from Compton, near Mount Gambier, and her toddler.
Crews are searching for a missing infant.
“Police have grave concerns for the child’s safety,” a South Australia police spokesperson said.
Detectives and forensic specialists are travelling to the scene.
Police are urging anyone who may have seen a white Isuzu MUX, registration S592BJR, to contact Crime Stoppers.

title: British YouTuber Yung Filly describes night he met fan in Australian nightclub before allegedly raping her
summary:
Performer on trial on six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent

A British YouTuber and musician accused of violently raping a fan after a gig never asked his alleged victim if she wanted sex, a court has been told.

Rapper Yung Filly, whose real name is Andrés Felipe Valencia Barrientos, is fighting six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent in a Perth hotel room in September 2024.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A British YouTuber and musician accused of violently raping a fan after a gig never asked his alleged victim if she wanted sex, a court has been told.
Rapper Yung Filly, whose real name is Andrés Felipe Valencia Barrientos, is fighting six charges of sexually penetrating a 20-year-old woman without consent in a Perth hotel room in September 2024.
The 30-year-old also denies impeding the woman’s breathing by applying pressure to her neck, and three counts of assault occasioning bodily harm.
His trial on Monday heard the performer met the woman at a nightclub called Bar1 after his performance.
“I fancied her and we got chatting,” Barrientos told the West Australian district court.
“The vibes were good, and she had a really good energy about her.”
The entertainer said he asked the woman if she wanted to come back to his hotel room while the pair were chatting in the VIP area of the nightclub. He said they later left in a minivan with his entourage and drove to the Intercontinental hotel in Perth’s CBD and the pair had consensual sex.
“The sex was great,” he said from the witness box.
Asked to describe the sex by his barrister, the rapper said there was “Grunting and moaning in a good way”.
He denied choking and slapping the woman, as has been alleged in the court. But he agreed he did bite her numerous times.
“In England we would call it a love bite. My mouth on her skin; it involves sucking [and] my teeth were involved to some extent.”
The jury has been shown images of the woman’s alleged injuries after the alleged assault. These include photos of deep bruising and bite marks on the woman’s face and neck.
Under cross-examination by prosecutor Danielle Clarke, Barrientos said he wasn’t surprised the woman came back to his hotel.
“I could just tell she was into me,” he said.
He agreed that when he asked her to leave with him, he didn’t mention having sex, but he believed they would do so. He said he initially grabbed the woman’s hand as they were leaving the nightclub about 3.30am, but let go.
“I quickly realised I didn’t want to be seen on socials,” he said.
The woman previously told the court Barrientos put his hands down her pants and touched her breast while they were in the club.
But the rapper denied the acts.
“It didn’t happen,” he said.
“I recall putting my hand on her waist.”
The entertainer also denied giving the woman tequila shots, contradicting the alleged victim’s evidence. He said these were handed around by the bar manager.
CCTV of the pair leaving the venue in Perth’s northern suburbs was played to the court. It showed Barrientos and other people getting into a white minivan and the woman following a short time later.
She paused at the door of the van before stepping in.
“All I remember is me leaving in front of her … and before I know it she was in the vehicle,” Barrientos said under questioning from his barrister.
The rapper didn’t recall whether the pair chatted during the drive to the hotel.
CCTV from the hotel showed him striding ahead of his entourage and the woman after they left the van. The group was then shown entering a lift.
“The vibes were good; we walked through the concierge and got into the lift … and I went into my room with [the woman],” Barrientos said.
The rapper agreed the woman’s phone was taken from her, as she alleged.
“It is standard practice for someone in the limelight to protect privacy,” he said.
The trial continues.

title: AstraZeneca boss urges western drugmakers to move at ‘Chinese speed’
summary:
Europe and US risk being outpaced on innovation, as happened in the car industry, warns Pascal Soriot

AstraZeneca must operate at “Chinese speed” to ensure it doesn’t suffer the fate of the western automotive industry by losing out to more innovative rivals, the drug company’s boss has said.

The FTSE 100 company is watching the rise of China’s pharmaceutical industry closely and collaborating to take drugs to global markets, but its chief executive, Pascal Soriot, said the US and European pharmaceutical sector must focus on increasing the speed of innovation.

Continue reading...
full_text:
AstraZeneca must operate at “Chinese speed” to ensure it does not suffer the fate of the western automotive industry by losing out to more innovative rivals, the drug company’s boss has said.
The FTSE 100 company is watching the rise of China’s pharmaceutical industry closely and collaborating to take drugs to global markets, but its chief executive, Pascal Soriot, said the US and European pharmaceutical sectors must focus on increasing the speed of innovation.
“We have to make sure we don’t fall behind,” Soriot said. “What we are learning ourselves is we have to move much faster. We always talk about Chinese speed in our company, and we want to operate in Chinese speed.”
AstraZeneca said on Monday it was confident of hitting its growth targets for 2030, when it expects to make $80bn (£60bn) in annual sales, up from $59bn last year. The British company, headquartered in Cambridge, reported revenues of £30.7bn in the first half of 2026, a 6% increase on the same period a year earlier at constant exchange rates.
Soriot, the highest-paid FTSE 100 chief executive, said the pipeline of new drugs from the company was “unmatched”, putting it on course to hit the growth targets in 2030 and beyond despite the surprise failure of Wainua, one of its major heart disease drug prospects, in clinical trials earlier this month.
“We have to accept to fail some of the time,” Soriot said. “Biology is biology.”
Despite confidence in growth prospects, French-born Soriot acknowledged that dominant pharmaceutical companies in Europe and the US needed to be aware of the potential challenge from Chinese competitors.
He cited the automotive industry as an example, where western companies had predominantly focused on making cars with petrol engines, leaving the way clear for Chinese companies to dominate electric car sales.
“Chinese companies were focused completely on electric vehicles and batteries and those kinds of technologies,” Soriot said, adding that Chinese pharmaceutical companies were investing heavily in equivalent novel technologies such as antibody drug conjugates, which deliver chemotherapy agents directly to cancer cells, and cell therapy, in which live cells are injected into the body to help fight diseases.
Sorit also played down the risk to jobs posed by AI, which he said could increase the speed of drug development, particularly in the design of trial protocols.
He said he believed AI tools would help improve productivity in the pharma industry, allowing for economic growth rather than meaning fewer people would be needed.
“This story about AI killing jobs is a bit of a fake story,” Soriot said. “I can tell you it makes me faster and smarter,” he added, of his experience interacting with AI tools.
Soriot said that AstraZeneca would engage with the UK government under its new leader, Andy Burnham, to seek clarity on a deal with the US that could result in the NHS paying billions of pounds more for medicines.
He said it was too early to say whether the change in leadership would have any effect on the deal – struck under pressure from Donald Trump, who threatened to impose heavy tariffs on UK drug exports to the US – which analysis has suggested could lead to 229,000 excess deaths in England.
“We need to understand their priorities and where the priorities are,” Soriot said. “You have to establish your priorities and then fund them.”

A French off-duty police officer has detained a man after he attacked and wounded three women with two kitchen knives in Paris on Monday.

full_text:
A French off-duty police officer has detained a man after he attacked and wounded three women with two kitchen knives in Paris on Monday.
Three women aged 19, 24 and 36 were taken to hospital after the assault at about 11.30am (0930 GMT) in the Porte de Clichy area in the north of the capital, said the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez.
Two had been gravely wounded but their lives were not in danger, Nuñez said. One had been injured in the lower back; the other in the abdomen.

The identity of the suspect and his motive were not immediately clear. Nuñez said he had made “incoherent statements”, but the minister advised against jumping to conclusions on the man’s motives.

title: Home Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza
summary:
Refugee family reunions in limbo, despite Foreign Office saying it is ready get people out of war-torn territory

The Home Office is blocking the evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza, despite the Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of the war-torn region.

Last September, the Home Office announced it was suspending refugee family reunion applications and that new, more restrictive rules would be announced in the spring. So far there has been no announcement and the process remains suspended.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Home Office is blocking the evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza, despite the Foreign Office saying it is ready to get people out of the war-torn region.
Last September, the Home Office announced it was suspending refugee family reunion applications and that new, more restrictive rules would be announced in the spring. So far there has been no announcement and the process remains suspended.
Applications made before the announcement continue to be processed. However, families in Gaza who applied to reunite with an immediate family member before the suspension have been blocked from joining loved ones in the UK.
The Home Office and the Foreign Office are involved in evacuations from Gaza. At the moment families who have a right to leave are evacuated via Jordan. However, the Home Office is not providing the required onward travel assurance (OTA) and is using legal challenges to block these families coming to the UK, sometimes deploying several senior barristers to a single case.
The Home Office says biometrics are obtained before families travel to Jordan, even though the visa centre in Gaza has been closed since October 2023. Other European countries such as Belgium, France, Italy and Ireland are facilitating such evacuations and the Foreign Office has said it is willing to evacuate the families.
Lawyers for the families stranded in life-threatening conditions in Gaza say the Home Office appears to be taking a harsher line with Palestinian families than with refugees from other countries hoping to reunite with loved ones in the UK. They say that in some cases the Home Office has stated that the family members, including small children, pose a security risk because they come from a “territory where terrorists operate”, even though some of the refugees in the UK were granted leave to remain on the basis of having been persecuted by Hamas in Gaza.
The Guardian has previously reported on the case of Bassem Abudagga, a PhD student who has been separated from his family. Although the Foreign Office has agreed to help with evacuating his family, the Home Office has said they will have to wait until December before officials make a decision about whether to grant an OTA.
In a communication with Abudagga’s lawyers on 15 July 2026 in response to descriptions of insanitary conditions, infested tents and frequent bombings, the Home Office said: “While this is acknowledged the conditions your clients face in Gaza alone are not considered to amount to compelling circumstances under the [relevant] guidance.”
In another case, a Palestinian refugee in the UK is separated from his wife, their three children – aged nine, 12, 14 – and his 17-year-old nephew who they adopted after the teenager was orphaned by the war.
He said: “My family are in constant danger and I worry about them every minute of every day. The UK government promised to help my family but has now gone back on that promise.
“They say my family could be dangerous because there are terrorists operating in Gaza. I don’t understand how a mother and her children can be considered a security threat. The Foreign Office has offered to evacuate my family, so why is the Home Office doing everything in its power to stop it?”
Sarah Crowe, a solicitor at the law firm Leigh Day representing some of the families trapped in the Palestinian territory and hoping to reunite with immediate family in Britain, said: “The UK government has abandoned vulnerable families in Gaza after promising to assist them. The Home Office is blocking family reunification when the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office is ready and willing to evacuate them.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Under our reforms to create a fairer asylum system, family reunion will no longer be automatic. Those seeking to bring family members to the UK will need to meet stricter criteria.”

title: Here’s the latest.
ICE Reportedly Set to Ramp Up Operations Against Haitian Migrants After TPS Ruling
summary: The potential crackdown follows a Supreme Court ruling that allowed the Trump Administration to end Haitians’ Temporary Protected Status.
full_text:
More than 300,000 Haitian immigrants are set to lose their ability to legally live and work in the U.S. on Monday, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is reportedly preparing to escalate its operations to arrest and deport some of them.
Those expanded operations could start as early as this week, according to reports from Fox News and CBS News, which cite unnamed federal sources. Ohio will reportedly be heavily targeted, particularly Springfield, where President Donald Trump had, in 2024, falsely accused Haitian migrants of eating residents’ pets.
A potential crackdown on Haitian migrants follows the Supreme Court’s June ruling that allowed the Trump Administration, for the time being, to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation for those fleeing violence and natural disaster in Haiti and Syria. The binding mandate of that ruling is expected to be transmitted to lower courts on Monday.
It remains unclear how aggressive the reported ICE campaign will be, and if Haiti can successfully reintegrate an influx of returnees. But Jean Négot Bonheur Delva, director-general of Haiti’s National Office of Migration, told local media earlier this month that following a conversation with the U.S. embassy in the country, Haitians should expect weekly deportation flights carrying about 250 former TPS status grantees.
The court ruling and its expected implementation have stirred anxiety among Haitians in the U.S. who could lose their livelihoods and may be sent back to the crisis-stricken Caribbean nation. It could also have a profound impact on the U.S. economy. A January 2026 fact sheet from immigration advocacy group FWD.us estimates that about 200,000 Haitian TPS holders are in the U.S. workforce, including 15,000 agricultural workers, 13,000 nursing assistants, and thousands of others in various industries.
In a statement to CBS News, DHS said it “does not discuss ongoing or future operations,” adding: “What we would say now is it’s closing time which means you don't have to go home, but you can't stay here… The good news is it's not too late to get a $2,600 check and a free flight home.”
Conditions in Haiti still severe
During his first-term Administration, Trump targeted TPS, a program since 1990 that has allowed migrants from designated countries with unsafe conditions—such as armed conflict, natural disaster, epidemics, or other extraordinary conditions—to reside and work legally in the U.S.
In his second-term Administration, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) moved to terminate TPS designations for several countries, including Ethiopia, Myanmar, and Yemen. In many announcements ending those protections, then-Secretary Kristi Noem emphasized that TPS was designed to be temporary, and she argued that the living conditions in many of the countries with TPS designation have improved. Any extension to the TPS designations for those countries, the department said, would be “contrary” to the “national interest.”
Persons who lose their TPS status must find another lawful basis for staying in the U.S. or depart the U.S.; otherwise they may be removed.
But these TPS rescissions and terminations have been legally challenged. In February, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Administration’s termination of Haiti’s TPS designation, though the Trump Administration appealed, eventually leading to the Supreme Court ruling.
Haiti first received a TPS designation in 2010 after a magnitude-7.0 earthquake struck the country in January that year, leaving more than 300,000 people dead and displacing over a million others. Since then, the country has been a TPS designee: the first-term Trump Administration’s planned termination was delayed mainly due to court injunctions and other rulings, and the succeeding Biden Administration renewed and extended those designations.
As DHS Secretary, Noem reviewed Haiti’s TPS designation and her department found that there were no “extraordinary and temporary conditions” that prevented Haitian nationals from returning safely, and that even if there were, allowing them to stay longer in the U.S. went against national interest.
The State Department, however, notes that conditions in the country are not that safe: as of July 10, it holds the highest-level travel warning to Americans, urging them not to visit. A state of national emergency has been in effect since 2024 because of gang-linked criminality and violence: an estimated 26 gangs, at times heavily armed, control 90% of the capital Port-au-Prince and its surrounding areas, and the nation’s government has had a hard time putting the situation under control.
According to the latest report by the International Organization for Migration, the violence in Haiti has displaced nearly 1.5 million persons, of whom more than half are women and girls.
‘A huge mistake’
Some Republicans have opposed the Trump Administration’s plan to end the TPS designation for Haiti.
In April, the GOP-controlled House passed legislation that would require the Homeland Security Secretary to redesignate Haiti to TPS until a few months into 2029, with 10 Republicans siding with Democrats. The legislation is now pending in the Senate, where the latest attempt to pass it was blocked on July 22 by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R, Mo.). But even if the bill passes both chambers, the White House earlier said that the President’s advisers would recommend vetoing it.
Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R, Fla.) told CBS News earlier this month that while Haiti is a “failed state,” he thinks “deporting Haitians that are under TPS right now, back to Haiti, would be a huge mistake.”
Markwayne Mullin, who took over for Noem as DHS Secretary in March, defended the decision to end Haiti’s TPS designation. Speaking to CNN in June, Mullin said that those staying in the U.S. under TPS have “had plenty of time” to explore other options to legally stay in the U.S. long-term, instead of banking solely on what was intended to be a temporary measure.
Asked about whether Haiti qualified as “safe,” Mullin told CNN that such a qualification “isn’t quite just that simple,” and he argued that the State Department travel advisory had Americans in mind and not Haitians.
“There isn’t a more generous country in the world than the United States,” Mullin said of the TPS designation, “but we don’t want people to take advantage of it.”

title: Hulu’s Riveting Revenge Thriller Furious Is Going to Haunt You
summary: Hulu's riveting revenge thriller interrogates the psychology of victimhood and the myth that the justice system protects the vulnerable.
full_text:
Midway through the Hulu thriller series Furious, it’s the middle of the night and two female FBI agents are on their way to investigate a lead when one notices the other’s bruises. “Who did that to your face?” demands Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine), who leads some of the Bureau’s most horrific sex crimes cases, as she pours liquor into her coffee cup. When Alice (Emmy Rossum), a rookie agent who worked as a Brooklyn homicide detective until her abusive, alcoholic cop boyfriend (Jake Lacy) ruined her police career, confesses that she met a man on the internet and asked him to hit her, she’s surprised to find her superior unfazed. “You think I’ve never let someone take a few whacks at this piñata?” Nora cracks. They both cackle.
If you find yourself laughing along with them—or can, at least, imagine why two women who have chosen to professionally immerse themselves in nightmarish sexual violence might seek a consensual version of it and also find the humor in that proclivity—then it’s likely you’ll be able to get on Furious’ wavelength. Created by Elizabeth Meriwether (Dying for Sex, New Girl) and premiering, with three episodes, on July 27, the series is more straightforward in its plot than the typical convoluted crime thriller but also more complex in its layered, often contradictory ideas. Its cat-and-mouse setup resembles that of Killing Eve: a troubled, underestimated female agent chases an eccentric, possibly psychopathic female killer. As its title suggests, one of its subjects is women’s rage. Yet, at its core, Furious is a haunting interrogation of the psychology of victimhood, the logic of revenge, and the myth that the justice system exists to protect the vulnerable, and its conclusions are too messy to resolve into a pat fable of empowerment or healing.
Although stickier questions of guilt and accountability arise, Meriwether doesn’t waste time on an initial murder mystery. Only after we watch a girlish woman in a cat mask (Say Nothing’s Lola Petticrew) administer a lethal injection to an incapacitated man, in between fetching candy for Brooklyn trick-or-treaters, do we meet the agent who will soon be on her trail. Having entered FBI training after her domestic violence allegations against Lacy’s Marshall made her a pariah at the precinct, Alice is pulled off desk duty at the Bureau to help investigate the Halloween murder. Behind that request is Dan (Scoot McNairy), the only NYPD detective still speaking to her and someone with whom she has quite a bit of history. (There aren’t many uncomplicated relationships in this show.) When the ad-hoc partners notice telling similarities between their new case—whose victim is the son of a billionaire, and whose female suspect has yet to be identified—and a year-old unsolved murder, Alice develops a theory that the two targets were involved in a child sex-trafficking ring and that their killer was one of the girls they trafficked.
She’s right, though that doesn’t make her investigation any easier. The murderer, whose name is Catherine but who goes by many other aliases, has a one-track mind set to revenge. Moving between domestic violence shelters and subsistence scams, she manipulates kindhearted nonprofit workers, nepo babies who fetishize her sex-worker past, and people who fall closer to the middle of the good-evil spectrum—whatever it takes to keep crossing names off her hit list. The collateral damage of Catherine’s quest can be devastating. Yet it’s hard to hate her. She’s clearly not a sociopath. She cares about children and is capable of authentic tenderness even when it serves no strategic purpose; when she harms innocent people, it palpably hurts her.
Just as Catherine is willing to inflict pain in the service of vengeance, Nora has resigned herself to absorbing it in the potentially fruitless service of justice. When Alice, who had previously asked to be assigned to Nora’s team, seeks her help on the case, the weary agent is locked in her office reviewing child sexual assault materials. “Why do you want to work in the basement on sex crimes and crimes against children?” Nora asks Alice. “Do you hate yourself? Don’t answer that.” By the time she playfully compares their heads to piñatas, we know that both women would, at least on some days, respond in the affirmative.
Nora harbors no illusions of heroism, which might explain why she drinks so much. Toward the end of the premiere, she dissects Medusa’s origin story for Alice, explaining that the mythical hag’s snakey mane was a punishment—imposed by Athena, no less—for the crime of being raped by Poseidon. “She’s a victim,” Nora says. “But it doesn’t make her a good person. It turns her into a monster.” Like Catherine. “Juries want to believe that women who are victims of violence,” she continues, “but in my experience being a victim of violence just makes you colder, more calculating. Victims of violence are the most violent.” Also? Justice is an impossible fantasy. “Anything you do, the ones who are really to blame don’t get caught. Never.”
Speeches like this often come at the end of today's bleaker crime dramas—”Forget it, Jake. It’s Chinatown,” but for viewers so distracted or dense, they need dialogue that spells out why Chinatown is a lost cause. Meriwether, whose best work interprets the motivations of apparently incomprehensible women like The Dropout’s Elizabeth Holmes and, in Dying for Sex, the real terminal cancer patient turned sexual explorer Molly Kochan, is doing something different. By placing Nora’s monologue so early in the series, then sending her all the way down the rabbit hole with Alice anyway, Furious is showing us a very smart person who has consciously committed to a lost cause. It’s also warning us against expecting the satisfying resolution, with villains punished and institutions redeemed, that draws so many people to detective stories.
In the seven episodes that follow, Meriwether piles on complications and thematic filters. There are parallels to the Epstein saga; tensions between an insular, blue-collar police force and federal agents with elite educations; systemic corruption; office politics. Bitter irony abounds, as when Nora, who is Black, attends a workplace mental health seminar in which a white, male supervisor who once mistreated her pretends to care about employees’ trauma. “What about anger?” she asks. Gender and race aren’t the only vectors of oppression the show considers. While wealth disparity plays pretty much exactly the role you’d expect, nuanced depictions of disability—particularly by Ramy actor Steve Way—challenge easy assumptions about personal agency in ways that relate to but are never conflated with the multiple abuse storylines.
As Nora’s speech and Catherine’s kind moments suggest, characters’ actions don’t consistently reflect their overall moral stance, which is often based on misunderstandings and falsehoods, its validity unknowable even to them. Being a woman, a survivor, or a person with physical differences doesn’t make a person righteous. Everyone you might consider a hero of this story will, at some point, do something abhorrent. “We become evil to fight evil,” says Nora, but if the most pernicious evildoers of all are uncatchable, how can the ends justify the means? Oscar contenders like Promising Young Woman and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri have also asked whether revenge, specifically as a response to sexual violence, can rebalance the moral universe, or if it’s ultimately suicidal. But both movies were glib thought experiments that distanced us from their characters to argue their points. Furious takes advantage of its longer runtime to get close to these people in pain. It never reduces them to cartoons.

title: 6 Easy Ways to Move More While Working from Home
summary: Even a little activity during the remote workday can help you focus, improve your mood and energy levels, and relieve stress.
full_text:
At most desk jobs, you’ll be sitting down for the majority of the day. But remote work creates a particularly sedentary environment. There’s no need to walk from your front door to the car or train station. There are no aisles of cubicles to maneuver on your bathroom break or colleagues to stand around with at the water cooler. “We're just sitting there in front of the screen by ourselves,” says Mary Jayne Rogers, an exercise physiologist based in Albuquerque, who’s on the certification advisory board of the American Council on Exercise.
This immobility has real downsides. “Prolonged sitting can increase the risk of heart disease and high blood pressure, even if you're otherwise active,” says Amy Bantham, past president of the Physical Activity Alliance. It also makes our fascia—the connective tissue that supports every structure, from our muscles and bones to our nerves and organs—stiffen up, causing ripple effects throughout the body that can impact our heart, lungs, gut, and even our brain, she says.
While giving yourself some adult recess during the work day might seem indulgent, it can actually make you more productive. Even a little activity can help you focus, improve your mood and energy levels, and relieve stress. “You will feel better almost immediately,” Bantham says.
Fortunately, remote work means there’s no one around to give you side-eye for doing jumping jacks between emails. Here are a few simple ways to move more when you’re working from home.
Create your own commute
During the time you’d otherwise spend commuting, Bantham suggests taking a walk. She runs her own consulting business from home and likes to go for a stroll and call a friend before work. Similarly, Lindsey Bomgren, a personal trainer based in Minneapolis, gets in her steps each morning while using her phone’s talk-to-text app to draft emails and write herself notes. “I can start my day out walking, wrapping my head around my to-do list,” she says.
Then, at the end of the day, Bomgren makes a point to do active errands around the house before her kids get home. “I’ll run up and down the stairs three times just to get laundry in, clean up, set out stuff for dinner,” she says. This gets her moving and helps her transition from work mode to mom mode.
Find ways to move while you work
Over the past few years, walking pads have become a popular way to boost your step count while at a computer. Some people, like Divya Balakrishnan, a yoga instructor in New York City, find the slow, rhythmic movement helps them stay focused and less stressed. “When something comes up, I'm a little bit more stable and able to handle it,” she says. Under-desk bikes and mini steppers are other options.
Another strategy is to use phone calls to go for a walk outside, pace the room, or simply stand up. “Even just standing extends your hip flexors, engages your glutes, engages your core,” Bomgren says.
If nothing else, Rogers suggests changing your posture throughout the day by shifting forward then back in your chair, or moving how you place your legs underneath you. Even bouncing your feet can increase circulation and move the joints a little. “The more you can keep things flowing, the more energy you're going to have at the end of the day,” she says.
Have an exercise snack
Taking a five-minute walk every hour has been shown to help offset the harms of sitting. Bantham says any quick movement break is worthwhile. “If you have two minutes between meetings, use those two minutes because it all counts,” she says.
That could look like a quick set of jump squats or crunches. It could mean running up and down the stairs as fast as you can. Or, for something even simpler, Rogers recommends standing up and sitting down 10 times.
Even gentle movement can help balance out hours of sitting, but if you’re using these “exercise snacks” in place of traditional workouts, Bomgren recommends making them hard enough to fatigue your muscles or become breathless. “You have to create enough external stress that it actually challenges you,” she says. She suggests aiming for about an eight or nine out of 10 difficulty level. If you push hard enough, research shows that short bursts of high-intensity movement can improve your cardiometabolic health and reduce your risk of several chronic diseases.
Schedule a lunchtime workout
One benefit of working from home is having a shower and a change of clothes handy. If you have the flexibility to do an online workout video or go for a run during your lunch hour, your afternoon might benefit. “It's like starting all over for the second half of the day so you've got less of that 4 p.m. lag where you feel like, ‘I need some coffee,’" Rogers says. Getting active shortly after lunch can also help regulate your blood sugar.
Stack habits
It’s easy to get caught up in emails and video meetings before realizing you haven’t budged in hours. To avoid this, Bomgren recommends pairing movement with things you do regularly during the work day. Maybe that’s getting in 10 push-ups anytime you fetch a cup of coffee, or stretching whenever you switch tasks.
Bantham says some of her clients intentionally schedule meetings to end five minutes before the top of the hour. That’s a natural chance to get up for a bathroom break and do some arm circles or calf raises—whatever your body is craving—before settling back down for the next call.
Don’t feel like you need to sweat
Rogers emphasizes that moving your body during the work day doesn’t need to be “exercise.” Even simple movements can encourage healthy blood flow and keep fascia from stiffening up. For instance, Balakrishnan suggests counteracting our hunched-over-the-keyboard posture with stretches that expand the chest (by reaching your arms overhead and back so your shoulders roll open), twist the spine (by grabbing one knee with the opposite hand), and open the hips (by laying one ankle across the opposite knee and reaching the chest forward). “You can do all of these from your chair, which makes it very hard to find an excuse to not do it,” she says. Although this won’t replace a workout, it can help break up sedentary hours.
The key is to find movements you enjoy enough to do consistently. “If you absolutely hate squats, don't choose squats to be the thing that you do between meetings,” Bantham says. Instead, maybe try a mini dance party to your favorite song, or release tension with a few deep breaths and neck rolls. It all helps. “Any activity is better than no activity,” Bantham says.

title: Chalk One Up for Ukraine
summary: Ukraine has built a defense sector at an astonishing speed and emerged as a global player in military innovation.
full_text:
It is often hard to know who is winning the war in Ukraine. The front lines scarcely budge. The air war brings regular Russian missile strikes—the most recent ones have hit Kyiv—and Ukrainian attacks that have battered Russian oil refineries and reached as far as Siberia. Ukrainian officials say the tide is turning their way; the Kremlin insists it will win a war of attrition.
In one significant way, Ukraine has already won. Some of the world’s wealthiest and most powerful nations—the United States included—are now turning to Ukraine for military assistance. Ukraine has built a defense sector at an astonishing speed and emerged as a global player in military innovation. “Ukraine needs NATO, but NATO needs Ukraine as much as the other way around,” remarked President Alexander Stubb of Finland, which joined NATO in 2023.
Beyond its implications for the war, this is a stunning achievement that will serve Ukraine well long after the guns fall silent. In President Donald Trump’s parlance, Ukraine now has a powerful “card” to play, a card it dealt itself.
From garage tech to global powerhouse
When Russia invaded Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky pleaded for foreign military aid from the West and exhorted his countrymen to build makeshift weapons for the resistance. For a time, Kyiv was grateful for pledges of American support, Bayraktar drones from Turkey, and whatever cheap weapons emerged from Ukrainian garages and warehouses.
Four and a half years later, American aid is drying up, Ukraine has replaced Bayraktar drones with more effective weapons of its own, and the country’s weapon designers have moved well beyond their low-tech garages. Ukraine’s defense technology sector is now a $7 billion industry, with many global customers and a projected annual production capacity estimated at $55 billion.
A short list of made-in-Ukraine successes includes the FP-5 Flamingo, a cruise missile with a range of more than 1,800 miles; tens of thousands of robots designed for frontline logistics and combat operations, which are minimizing risk for soldiers and are increasingly used for holding ground, firing on the enemy, and even taking prisoners; drones launched from unmanned boats to intercept and destroy Russian Shahed drones; and the “Lima” electronic warfare system, which spoofs satellite navigation signals, sending incoming missiles astray.
What began as a frantic request for outside help and garage-style innovation has evolved into a manufacturing juggernaut, large enough to support the resistance and to sell to other nations. “I’ve been arguing for many years that Ukraine would eventually become a net exporter of security,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. Ambassador to Russia, remarked in April. “That day is coming faster than I imagined.”
How the Iran war has helped Ukraine
The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran hurt Ukraine by shifting global attention away from Russia’s aggression, but that war has also been a boon for Kyiv. Gulf states, and even some American military bases in the region, turned out to be poorly prepared to fight Iranian drone and missile attacks. Ukraine had built the technology that could help.
Ukraine’s edge involves what some have called the “Ford-versus-Ferrari” problem in air defense. The U.S. and its allies in the Gulf have relied on the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) and Patriot missile defense systems, which can knock almost any incoming weapon out of the sky. But those systems were designed to counter heavy missiles, and they are expensive. Each Patriot missile costs roughly $5 million. Using these against $50,000 Iranian drones is, as many have noted, akin to racing a Ferrari against a Ford. Rep. Ted Lieu, a Democrat from California, compared it to “throwing Ferraris at frisbees.”
Enter Ukraine, with its battle-tested counter-drone systems, which have beaten back barrages of Russian and Iranian drones at a fraction of the cost of THAAD systems and Patriots. To extend the metaphor, these are “Fords.” And they work. Zelensky has made this case to the rest of the world with great effect. In the past few months, he has signed defense export agreements with Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar, wealthy nations that typically turn to the U.S. for military hardware.
Washington has gone from dismissing Zelensky to seeking deals of its own with Ukraine. After an Iranian drone attack killed six American soldiers in Kuwait in March, the Trump Administration turned to Ukraine for help. At Washington’s request, Ukraine set up its Sky Map air defense system at Saudi Arabia’s Prince Sultan Air Base, home to more than 2,000 Americans. Two months later, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll said he was pushing American firms to develop low-cost air defense interceptors within a year, and encouraged them to learn from the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
At a White House meeting last August, according to Axios, Zelensky presented a plan to exchange Ukrainian counter-drone technology for American aid. His PowerPoint included a scenario that would turn out to be prescient: Iranian drone attacks on the Gulf states and American military bases in the region. The White House rejected the offer. Even in March, Trump was dismissive, saying: “We don’t need their help in drone defense.”
Though Ukraine still cannot envision a path into NATO, it is now selling its weapons and expertise to NATO countries and advising the alliance on military matters. During NATO exercises on Sweden’s Gotland island in May, Ukrainian drone teams overwhelmed Swedish forces, and warned the alliance that it was unprepared for modern drone warfare.
Ukraine has opened ten weapons export centers across Europe. On July 15, the European Union and Ukraine signed a drone-production partnership. Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland announced a deal under which Ukraine would help his country build a “modern drone Armada.” Ukraine and Germany have signed an agreement focusing on drone production and battlefield technology integration. And Kyiv has signed drone deals with Norway, Denmark, and the Baltic nations. Even Japan is getting in on the Ukrainian boom: its Terra Drone company has partnered with a Ukrainian developer to scale up interceptor drone systems.
A powerful card
None of this guarantees Ukraine a victory over Russia, or even success at the negotiating table. What it does do is boost the odds that, when the guns finally fall silent, Ukraine will have a viable future and a powerful post-war “card” to play.
Were the war to end tomorrow, Ukraine would have lost territory but gained military partnerships and significant investments, along with a new engine for its security and economic future. Russia, meanwhile, would struggle to reassemble an economy that has been badly battered, one that relies almost solely on the fickle oil market and the war economy itself.
All of which is to say: chalk one up for Ukraine. These aren’t just wins for Kyiv’s coffers, or for its ability to wreak fresh havoc on Russian targets. They are also a valuable asset that isn’t going anywhere, no matter what happens on the battlefield. For a country that will need every possible resource to rebuild, that is not just a card. It is an ace.

title: The Contradiction at the Heart of Disability in America
summary: America loves seeing disabled people. It doesn’t want to pay to keep us alive, writes Steve Way.
full_text:
I’m an actor. I also use a motorized wheelchair and a ventilator, and both of them run on Medicaid. The machine that pushes air into my lungs, the chair that moves me across a room, and the aide who gets me out of bed so I can do my job and be on television are all paid for by Medicaid. Without that coverage, I wouldn’t have a career. Instead, I would have a massive life crisis.
I’ve spent this year in a split-screen. On one side, I’ve had the best professional run of my life. On the other, a law that’s starting to take shape is threatening to make people like me suffer and disappear.
That contradiction ultimately comes down to how much our country believes a disabled person is worth.
On July 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. By the Congressional Budget Office’s own accounting, its Medicaid provisions cut around $1 trillion in federal spending over a decade, and will leave an estimated 7.5 million more people uninsured by 2034. Count the rest of the law’s health provisions, and the coverage loss climbs to an estimated $10 million. The Center for American Progress notes the spending cuts almost exactly match the law’s other half: about $1 trillion in tax cuts flowing to the top 1% of households, nearly half of that to roughly 200,000 households making more than $2 million a year.
Approximately a trillion dollars taken from the care of poor and disabled people, and roughly a trillion handed to the richest households in the country.
Then, there’s the cost no budget table ever lists. Before the bill reached its final, larger form, three physician-researchers published a peer-reviewed analysis in the Annals of Internal Medicine projecting what the cuts would do to actual lives. Their mid-range estimate:16,642 additional preventable deaths a year.
If the losses fall hardest on disabled, high-cost enrollees rather than spreading evenly, the cuts could go even deeper. In a law built to find savings, the most expensive bodies to keep alive are the most efficient place to look. The math suggests that I cost a lot, and the bill was written by people looking for things that cost a lot.
We must not trade disabled peoples’ lives in exchange for tax cuts for the ultra-wealthy. And we must not sacrifice all of the progress the U.S. has made.
On July 26, 1990, a Republican president signed the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), the world’s first comprehensive civil rights law for disabled people, and a law older than me. George H.W. Bush stood on the South Lawn and promised disabled people “independence, freedom of choice, control of their lives, the opportunity to blend fully and equally into the rich mosaic of the American mainstream.”
Yesterday marked its 36th anniversary. The show I’m proudly in, Furious, premieres today.
The ADA said disabled people have a right to live in America. The new law cuts the exact funding that helps many of us live, including the home-based services that keep disabled people like myself out of nursing facilities and in their own homes, which is the precise independence the ADA was written to protect.
Representation has quietly become a consolation prize. Even though the percentage is still low, there are more disabled people on television than ever, and I’m grateful to be one of them. But the applause and the cuts are happening simultaneously, to the same people, and almost no one with power experiences that as a contradiction.
You can be celebrated on a streaming service and defunded by a signature in the same summer. The issue: being seen is not the same as being kept alive.
Many people genuinely believe those are the same thing. Visibility is a form of protection and a society putting disabled people on television would surely not also strip away the thing that gets them out of bed. It’s a comforting belief, but in modern America, it is false. Visibility is cheap. It costs the country nothing. Care is what costs, and care is what was cut.
America has gotten very good at the gesture of inclusion and very comfortable with the substance of abandonment. Too often, we perform the first loudly enough to drown out the second.
Disabled people see this gap with clarity. I’m telling you what it looks like from here because the view is unobstructed, and because I am, for now, still in a position to describe it.
I’ll spend this month promoting a television show, marking 36 years of a promise, and watching my own healthcare coverage get more precarious, doing the arithmetic on my care in the back of my mind while I smile for cameras. I’ve got some great red carpet one-liners lined up.
I’ve built a career on finding the joke in exactly this kind of absurdity, and I have to find it here, because the alternative is worse.

title: What to Know About the Deadly Wildfires in Western Europe
summary: More than 300,000 people were evacuated because of wildfires in France and Spain, with fire crews battling the blazes for several days.
full_text:
More than 300,000 people were evacuated and at least one person killed because of wildfires in France and Spain, with fire crews battling the blazes for several days.
The two countries are facing massive wildfires that began last week amid successive heat waves in Europe that produced record high temperatures in several countries and led to thousands of excess deaths.
In France, a major fire broke out in Saumos in Gironde last Wednesday, and a separate fire began near Biscarrosse in the Landes department the next day. Several fires broke out in Spain last Wednesday, including one in Toledo that spread into Madrid’s Villa del Prado and another in Ávila. Fires in Madrid, Castellón, and Manises broke out in the following days.
Both countries had already faced deadly wildfires earlier in the summer.
Here’s what to know about the wildfires affecting France and Spain.
What has been the impact?
Fire crews were dealing with a 280-km perimeter of fire covering 77,000 hectares across Madrid, Ávila, and Toledo, Spain’s Secretary-General for Civil Protection and Emergencies Virginia Barcones told state broadcaster TVE.
The Spanish regions of Madrid, Ávila, and Valencia were among the worst affected areas. The government declared a national emergency in Madrid and Ávila on Thursday evening, extending it to Toledo on Saturday. It was Spain’s first such declaration over wildfires and only the second overall, after the nationwide blackout in April 2025. The government deployed 1,200 and 400 vehicles to fight the fires in Madrid and Ávila, respectively. At least 37 sections of road were closed to traffic on Sunday morning because of fires across seven provinces or regions.
Spain recorded its first death from the latest wildfires on Saturday when a 78-year-old man was killed in a fire in Manises, near Valencia. The victim, who reportedly had reduced mobility, was found dead in his car.
Several major fronts of the wildfires affecting Madrid and Ávila were contained by Sunday morning, according to Spain’s Military Emergencies Unit, although the fires remained active. The wildfire risk also remained high in the eastern and southern parts of the country, according to Spain’s meteorological agency, Aemet. That risk is expected to go up in the coming days as the temperature warms this week, Aemet said.
In France, around 55,000 people were ordered to evacuate villages near Bordeaux, including Le Barp, Marcheprime, Biganos, Mios, and Cestas, overnight on Saturday. In total, more than 250,000 people in southwestern France were forced to evacuate in recent days.
In Gironde, at least 240 homes were destroyed as of Sunday, officials said. The fire spread to within 15 km from the edge of Bordeaux’s metropolitan area and around 25 to 30 km from the city center. Bordeaux officials said they are evaluating the situation but that there are no immediate plans to evacuate the city.
Wildfires in France have also disrupted the Tour de France, as organizers shortened its final stage from 133 km to 89 km so security personnel can be redeployed to affected areas.
France’s meteorological agency warned that wildfire danger remained high across many departments despite a slight improvement over the weekend, especially as another heat wave is expected to worsen fire conditions in the coming days.
How is climate change exacerbating wildfire risks?
Much of Europe has been affected by successive heat waves that have raised the risk of wildfires. With temperatures expected to rise again and little rain forecast in many fire-affected areas, that danger is only expected to increase this week.
Global warming has made heat waves more prevalent and more intense, with Europe warming at twice the global average rate since the 1980s. The extreme heat increases evaporation and plant water loss, worsening drought and drying out vegetation which creates more fuel for wildfires.
Spain recorded 32 major forest fires so far this year. That’s a significant increase from last year, when the country recorded seven over the same time period.
“I’d once again like to urge people to take utmost care and to stay up to date,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Sunday. “The Iberian Peninsula is suffering the effects of the climate emergency.”
Heat waves also make it more difficult to contain fires, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told La Tribune Dimanche on Sunday. Dry weather, high temperatures, and dense ground vegetation make the fires spread rapidly once they begin.
Earlier this month, other deadly wildfires struck France and Spain. At least 13 people were killed in the Los Gallardos fire in southern Spain and a 22-year-old volunteer firefighter died while battling a vegetation fire in Savoie, France.
How to stay safe
People in affected areas should follow official instructions and evacuate immediately if ordered.
Anyone in the E.U. who suspects a new fire should call 112 if it is safe to do so, and move away from the flames toward an area with little vegetation. If smoke or ash is present, residents should limit outdoor activities.
The Madrid regional government said, as of Sunday, 2,468 evacuees were receiving assistance at 15 temporary shelters, where local authorities supplied meals, beds, and basic hygiene products.
French municipalities have also opened temporary shelters. Bordeaux officials said around 3,500 evacuees were staying at its exhibition center shelter on Saturday morning.
