title: Five years after Saied’s power grab, Tunisians are no better off
summary: Tunisia has seen no economic benefit from power consolidation, while liberties have dwindled.
full_text:
Five years after Saied’s power grab, Tunisians are no better off
Tunisia has seen no economic benefit from power consolidation, while liberties have dwindled.
On July 27, 2021, Tunisian President Kais Saied suspended parliament in what was then considered the Arab world’s only functioning constitutional democracy. As the United States’ acting assistant secretary of state for Near East Affairs, I was sent on a mission along with Deputy National Security Advisor Jon Finer to ascertain Saied’s plans. Then-US President Joe Biden had expressed his hope to see a swift return to parliamentary democracy, and for the naming of a prime minister and a government that could address the country’s looming economic problems.
During our meeting, President Saied asked Mr Finer and me to reassure President Biden that he was merely responding to the popular will to end a culture of bribery and corruption, and his actions were meant to fully implement the country’s constitution. He did not indicate when or if a new prime minister would be named, a new constitution would be promulgated, or if he viewed the parliament as temporarily suspended or disbanded entirely.
To see if we could better understand President Saied’s intentions, we requested to meet with his closest adviser, Nadia Akacha, over lunch. Pointing to Tunisians having fun on a nearby beach, Ms Akacha told us, “You see? They are not unhappy with President Saied’s decision to take the reins of leadership. They want change. They want someone whom they can hold accountable.”
Five months later, Ms Akacha would resign, and within a year, she would be on the run from the law, denying all accusations and denouncing Saied’s consolidation of power. As for the kind of change she and many Tunisians were expecting, they are still waiting for it five years later.
In response to President Saied’s measures, the US government slashed its military assistance allocation to Tunisia by 50 percent as a signal to both Congress and the Tunisian leadership that all was not well in the bilateral relationship.
On February 1, 2023, the Biden administration sent me to Tunis as ambassador with instructions to find ways to help put Tunisia back on a pathway to representative democracy.
Less than two weeks later, I confronted a crisis: virtually all the country’s political party leaders were arrested. Soon a similar crackdown on civil society leaders and the press followed.
In the coming years, Tunisians lost a great deal of their civil liberties. The country’s score in Freedom House’s “Freedom in the World” index fell from 70 to 42 between 2020 and 2026, with lower scores reflecting less freedom.
At the same time, Tunisians gained nothing in economic performance. Tunisia’s real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 2026 and unemployment are no better than they were in 2018, the year before President Saied came to power, while its debt-to-GDP ratio has grown from around 73 percent to over 81 percent.
President Saied nonsensically rejected as “foreign diktats” the subsidy reform programme that his own government presented to the International Monetary Fund and that won support from the US government, among others.
Meanwhile, with ministerial longevity hovering around six months, Tunisian officials could never be sure what their president wanted, or what would cause them to be fired. When I asked the CEO of a major American energy company what he wanted from Tunisia as a priority, he said, “A phone number with someone on the other end.”
Bilateral security cooperation offered the one bright spot over the past five years, perhaps because US military assistance comes in the form of grants, training, and exercises, not loans with the type of conditionality President Saied sees as “diktats”. As a result, the Tunisian security services have had all the support they need to rid the country of virtually every known terrorist cell, which is quite an achievement given the instability that racked the country previously.
Perhaps therein lies a way forward for the United States and Tunisia’s other traditional partners. They can take advantage of the security infrastructure in which the US and Tunisia invested hundreds of millions of dollars together since 2014 to help provide similar training and exercises to security forces from the Sahel nations, who so desperately need it to stabilise their own countries.
The Tunisians can deliver all of this far less expensively than the US can on its own, and it would likely be more welcome among African governments than an initiative coming solely from Washington in the current global context.
Whatever direction in which Tunisians decide to take their country in the coming five years, they will need security and stability not just at home, but in their neighbourhood as well. If the US and Tunisia’s other traditional partners remain engaged on these most fundamental goals, this will provide the Tunisian people the environment they need to find their own ways to rebuild their political and economic lives.
In the current circumstances, the United States and others can at the very least help ensure that President Saied’s inability to spur economic growth or tolerate political pluralism does not drive the country into an even more desperate situation.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Australian court rejects racial discrimination appeal by Pauline Hanson
summary: ⁠Court upholds earlier ruling ⁠that a post directed at Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi was unlawful.
full_text:
Australian court rejects racial discrimination appeal by Pauline Hanson
Court upholds earlier ruling that post directed at Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi was unlawful.
An Australian court has unanimously rejected an appeal by right-wing leader Pauline Hanson to overturn a ruling that she racially discriminated against a Muslim senator.
In 2024, Hanson was found to have violated racial discrimination laws after she told Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi to “pack your bags and p*** off back to Pakistan”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Argentina fans accused of violence, racism by Egypt, Cape Verde supporters
- list 2 of 3Andy Burnham’s in-tray: The challenges facing the new UK PM
- list 3 of 3Austria turns Adolf Hitler’s birthplace into police station
The leader of the anti-migrant One Nation party had made the comment in a social media post two years earlier, on the day Britain’s Queen Elizabeth II died, while responding to Faruqi’s remarks that she could not “mourn the leader of a racist empire built on stolen lives, land and wealth of colonised peoples”.
In their ruling on Monday, the three-judge panel of the Full Federal Court of Australia said that “none of the grounds” of appeal had been established, adding that Hanson’s comment was unlawful and unprotected by free speech defences.
“Today, justice has prevailed,” Faruqi told reporters outside court in Sydney. “Today’s win is for every single person out there who has been told to go back to where you came from.”
Hanson said she and her legal team would review the decision and intended to lodge an appeal with Australia’s final court of appeal, the High Court.
“Public discussion in Australia has become almost totally silenced by laws and rules which prevent ordinary people expressing their personal views in case some small part of our society takes some sort of offence or feels hurt or ‘distressed’. This has never been, nor ever should be, the Australian way,” Hanson posted on X.
The Full Federal Court said it agreed with the 2024 judgement, which “correctly characterised” Hanson’s post as containing an anti-Muslim and Islamophobic message and “being a variant of the historically racist, nativist and anti-immigrant slogan ‘go back to where you came from’.”
The law was also constitutionally valid and Hanson did not establish a defence allowing for fair comment on a matter of public interest, it said.
“We have 434 paragraphs of dismissing Pauline Hanson’s appeal, of confirming that indeed Pauline Hanson behaved in racism, Islamophobia, and hate,” Faruqi said.
“Hate speech is not free speech, and the Federal Court has reaffirmed that today.”
Founded in 1997, One Nation was long seen as a fringe party but Hanson’s hard line on immigration has attracted more support in recent polls.
Hanson has advocated for an end to multiculturalism in Australia, saying the country should exist as a “monocultural” society.

title: Israel’s approval of limited Gaza force a calculated manoeuvre, experts say
summary: Analysts say Israeli cabinet's decision aims to deflect US pressure and fragment the Gaza Strip.
full_text:
Israel’s approval of limited Gaza force a calculated manoeuvre, experts say
Analysts say the Israeli cabinet’s decision aims to deflect US pressure and fragment the Gaza Strip.
Months after the United Nations Security Council backed a comprehensive framework to end Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Israel’s security cabinet has approved a highly constrained pilot project to allow foreign security forces into a narrow pocket of the devastated territory.
Israeli media reported on Sunday that the so-called International Stabilization Force (ISF), part of United States President Donald Trump’s 20-point “peace plan”, will include 200 members from countries such as Morocco and Uganda deploying to a designated “test” zone in the southern city of Rafah.
While international officials have welcomed the move, analysts describe the limited deployment as a calculated diplomatic gesture with little practical effect that comes as the US-backed peace process has largely stalled and as Israel’s deadly attacks continue.
Instead of a genuine transition towards peace, they argue, the move is a political manoeuvre designed to deflect US pressure ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to Washington this week, while simultaneously entrenching the geographic fragmentation of the Gaza Strip.
“Netanyahu is going to Washington to say ‘no’ to the broader demands of withdrawal” from the Strip, says Wissam Afifa, a Gaza-based political analyst. “Instead, he is offering this alternative: ‘Take this small appetiser, take this minor achievement, and play within this highly restricted space.'”
Scaled-back forces and ‘rubber batons’
The Israeli daily Haaretz reported that the original plan anticipated the deployment of 500 Moroccan troops to a refugee camp in the city. The drastic reduction to just 200 troops may indicate that Israel’s political-security cabinet has decided to divide the deployment into even smaller, heavily controlled stages.
The force will operate in full coordination with the Israeli military. According to the Israeli news outlet Ynet, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir was the sole cabinet member to vote against the measure, arguing that the Palestinian group Hamas had failed to fulfill its commitment to disarm and insisting that “the solution in Gaza is to encourage migration”.
Israeli media also reported that the government maintains that the Israeli military will retain control of the “Yellow Line” – a unilaterally imposed boundary that effectively places up to 70 percent of the Gaza Strip under tight Israeli control – and that no withdrawal will take place until Hamas has fully disarmed.
The original framework endorsed by UNSC Resolution 2803 called for the deployment of an international force alongside a transitional Palestinian administration.
Earlier this month, Hamas announced it would dissolve its government in Gaza and hand over power to a new, Palestinian technocratic governing authority called the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Analysts said Hamas’s move was likely designed to apply pressure on Israel and demonstrate the group’s commitment to handing over governance and allowing the rebuilding of the territory.
The pilot programme also envisions the NCAG’s entry to oversee civil affairs in Gaza. Yet, according to Haaretz, the Palestinian police accompanying them will be stripped of firearms, permitted to carry only “rubber batons and tasers”.
Meanwhile, preparations on the ground appear to be moving forward to accommodate this new security architecture. Israeli Army Radio recently broadcast a video showing a military base under construction in the southern “Gaza envelope” near the Karem Abu Salem (Kerem Shalom) crossing.
The station reported that the sprawling facility is being built specifically to host the incoming multinational forces before their deployment.
Despite the severe Israeli restrictions, Nickolay Mladenov, the high representative for the Board of Peace, welcomed the Israeli cabinet’s decision, praising it as a “critical part of the agreed framework for stabilizing Gaza, supporting demilitarization, and enabling the transition to effective Palestinian transitional administration”.
A ‘sweetener’ for Washington
To understand the timing and motivation behind the decision, experts pointed to the diplomatic deadlock surrounding the US-brokered peace initiative. Trump’s plan envisioned a phased approach, bridged by the handover of Gaza to a technocratic committee. However, this framework has been stalled by Israel’s refusal to link a ceasefire to the broader political situation and its rejection of a phased withdrawal.
Afifa said the “failure” of the US administration’s flagship initiative had left it “embarrassed” as the project that was repeatedly highlighted by Trump “as a great achievement, resulted in zero”.
With Netanyahu heading to Washington, the Israeli prime minister desperately needed a deliverable, said Afifa. The cabinet’s decision, passed hastily via a telephone vote during a Knesset recess to avoid internal coalition fractures, provides exactly that, he added.
Mamoun Abu Amer, an expert on Israeli affairs, echoed this assessment. He viewed the rushed cabinet vote as an attempt to preempt US pressure and present an image of compliance to Trump, while fundamentally altering the agreement’s core terms to suit Israel’s long-term security strategy.
Abu Amer also said that Israel has effectively turned Resolution 2803 upside down through selective and highly conditional implementation.
“This is an inverted process,” said Abu Amer. The original text implied that the NCAG would enter Gaza, the ISF would deploy and the Israeli military would withdraw to new lines to allow for stabilisation. Instead, Israel is demanding unilateral disarmament first, while keeping the technocratic committee besieged within an Israeli security envelope.
Abu Amer also suggested the requirement for the Palestinian police force to only carry rubber batons and tasers reflects a premeditated Israeli strategy to strip the Palestinian administration of genuine law enforcement capabilities, reducing them to subcontractors managing municipal decay in a thoroughly devastated environment under a strict military occupation.
The NCAG itself appeared to reject this Israeli paradigm. In a recent statement, the committee declared it would only assume responsibility for Gaza after UNSC approval of the force’s deployment and, crucially, a full Israeli military withdrawal.
‘False witnesses’
The spatial realities of the Israeli plan reveal a strategy of deep fragmentation and long-term control, experts said, pointing to the cabinet’s decision to explicitly restrict the ISF and the technocrats to operating strictly outside the “Yellow Line”.
Afifa warned that transforming a small pocket of Rafah into an “experimental bubble” subverts the idea of Gaza as a single, contiguous territorial entity.
“This raises a massive question about the fate of two million people,” he said. “If this entire project is reduced to a few thousand individuals selected under Israeli criteria, it means a tacit agreement from the international community to leave two million Gazans hostage to a catastrophic humanitarian crisis while Israel claims to be implementing a peace plan.”
This also carries significant diplomatic risks for the participating nations. Israeli media reported the cabinet’s decision stipulated that ISF contributors must be nations that have peace agreements with Israel and do not pursue legal actions against it in international forums.
“It is not wise for an Arab country like Morocco to be a party to helping Netanyahu implement his political agenda,” said Abu Amer, urging participating nations to reject the altered Israeli formula and insist on a comprehensive withdrawal.
Failing to do so, he cautioned, would reduce foreign troops to mere security buffers, acting as “false witnesses” to the continuation of the occupation and the destruction

title: Three killed in suspected shootout in US city of Seattle, police say

Three killed in suspected shootout in US city of Seattle, police say
Police say one suspect surrendered at the scene of the shooting, while the other remains on the loose.
Three people have been shot dead at a crowded food festival in Seattle in the United States. Four others were wounded, including a toddler, in what city police believe was a shootout involving two suspects.
One of them surrendered to police after the shooting on Sunday – the other fled.

Assistant Seattle Police Chief Tyrone Davis told a news conference on Sunday night that there was no ongoing threat to the public, but added that police did not have a description of the suspect who remained on the run.
“We’re still trying to figure this out,” Davis said.
Police said the suspect in custody was a “young person” but declined to provide more details.
The gunshots at the Bite of Seattle food festival beneath the famous Space Needle were heard at around 6pm local time (01:00 GMT Monday).
“What happened here today at the Seattle Center was an unbelievable tragedy and a horrific act of violence,” Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said at the news conference.
“We have far too much gun violence in this city and in this country, and we’re coming off of a week in Seattle where we’ve had three major incidents of gun violence in just a few days.”
Police said the dead were two men, aged 19 and 44, and a 56-year old woman. The wounded, including a two-year-old boy, were in a stable condition in hospital.

title: Students and staff work to bring Islamic University of Gaza back to life
summary: The university is looking to continue educating Palestinians amid Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
full_text:
Students and staff work to bring Islamic University of Gaza back to life
The university is looking to continue the education of Palestinians amid the destruction brought about by Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.
Before the war, the Islamic University of Gaza was one of the leading public universities in the Palestinian enclave.
Despite the challenges of Israeli air attacks and a siege on Gaza, it worked to provide the best possible academic environment for students.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Can AI systems make moral decisions in war?
- list 2 of 4What does Khalil al-Hayya’s election win mean for Gaza?
- list 3 of 4Head of police in northern Gaza killed in Israeli strike

Of particular focus were fields relying heavily on practical training, such as medicine, health sciences and engineering. But Israel’s crippling hold on Gaza posed huge challenges in teaching these disciplines.
Still, students spent hours in laboratories, working with medical equipment, handling samples and applying what they had learned theoretically in classrooms to ready themselves for futures in science, medicine and engineering.
All this changed on October 8, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began. It saw university campuses bombed and a tightening of a siege that restricted the entry of even pens and notebooks.
Yassin al-Nounou, the university’s laboratory coordinator, said equipment to support medical and health sciences had arrived just days before the war began.
It included anatomy models and educational skeletons to strengthen practical training and bring students closer to real workplace environments. These plans came to a halt when the university lost a significant part of its infrastructure, laboratories and equipment when massive Israeli bombing began.
Even the latest “ceasefire”, beginning in October 2025, repeatedly violated by Israel, has brought a new challenge: how to rebuild education for students from rubble?
Days of disaster
As many as 19 educational buildings were destroyed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, while about 500 classrooms, 200 scientific laboratories and 75 computer laboratories were also severely damaged. The central library lost more than 240,000 books, journals, references and academic theses.
Abdulraouf Ali al-Manama, dean of the university’s health sciences faculty, describes the past three years as “one of the greatest disasters in the university’s history”.
Israeli bombing destroyed most academic buildings, classrooms, educational and research laboratories, libraries and training clinics. The university lost thousands of scientific devices, laboratory materials, books and resources it had accumulated over the past five decades. What remained was “the ruins of a destroyed university”, al-Manama said.
The mass displacement from Gaza’s towns and cities also saw campus buildings and facilities converted into temporary shelters. Shortages of suitable classrooms, repeated electricity and internet outages, and the psychological and social toll experienced by students and staff have severely affected the university’s ability to teach, he said.
Amid a devastated landscape and roadblocks, students are still struggling to reach the university or training locations, making education a difficult practical journey in itself.
The war also represented the loss of an integrated educational environment to provide students, particularly in medicine and sciences, with the professional skills needed to help Gaza function.
An assessment by the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education, in cooperation with UNESCO, showed that most higher education institutions in Gaza sustained significant damage since 2023. Hundreds of specialised laboratories and facilities have lost their ability to operate.
The use of laboratories, medical equipment, handling samples, conducting tests and analysing results is what connects students’ theoretical knowledge to real-life cases.
Destruction of these facilities means that many courses reliant on practical training can now only be taught theoretically.
One alternative has been to use digital simulations and recorded experiments in teaching medical microbiology, biochemistry, haematology, molecular diagnostics, medical optics laboratories, and physical therapy training.
These solutions provide a temporary fix to the problem. But al-Manama said they cannot replace real laboratories that are essential to help students gain practical skills and the confidence needed to practise what they have learned.
Between the classroom and hospital
Deema Muhaisen, a medical student, has seen her education transform dramatically since the university laboratories were destroyed. She says before the war, she would spend hours in the laboratory developing the skills needed to become a doctor.
Since the destruction of the medicine faculty on December 9, 2023, she no longer has a fixed place to study, and much of her learning has now shifted to hospitals and healthcare settings.
“In many cases, we received lectures in hospital corners and between patient rooms, gathered around doctors, in places that did not provide the minimum requirements for an educational environment,” she said.
“The thing I missed the most was regular clinical interaction with patients under academic supervision, because this experience is the foundation for building a medical student’s skills and confidence.”
But the priority for the doctors, who effectively became Muhaisen’s teachers, was treating injured patients. There was also limited space in overcrowded hospitals for training students.
Muhaisen tried to compensate for this by helping doctors in hospitals to gain some practical experience. For two years, she volunteered in emergency departments, wound care units and surgery departments at several hospitals across northern and southern Gaza, beginning with simple tasks, but developing into greater responsibilities as the need for medical staff increased.
“I began assisting in operating rooms, following up with many patients after surgeries, and responding to their needs and concerns,” she said. “This gave me deep practical experience and strengthened my sense of responsibility.”
Yassin al-Nounou, the university’s laboratory coordinator, says besides the loss of the equipment, there is also a gap between students’ theoretical knowledge and practical experience via laboratories and learning to use medical equipment in a classroom setting.
“Students used to study the device, understand its details, how it operates, and how to use it, so they would be able to work with it when entering the job market,” he said. “Today, there is no equipment and no laboratory like the ones that existed before.”
The university was forced to rely on theoretical explanations, videos, and recorded experiments to deliver this information to students.
“During this period, students began to feel anxious because they asked: ‘How will we work with something we have never seen in reality? How will we handle a device we have never stood in front of or used with our own hands?’” al-Nounou said.
To reduce this gap, the university coordinates with healthcare centres, hospitals and local institutions so students can combine the theoretical and practical aspects of their studies in a real-life setting.
Reintroducing teaching
Despite the scale of destruction to its faculties, the Islamic University is still looking for ways to gradually resume in-person lectures when the situation allows.
Al-Nounou, the lab coordinator, says the destruction of the main campus is an obvious obstacle to reintroducing in-person lectures.
There are few buildings available on the campus for teaching, and many of the standing structures are still being used as shelters for displaced Palestinians.
To respond to this, the university has established five branches and educational facilities across different parts

With less than three months to go until Brazil’s presidential election, China is closely watching a high-stakes political duel between a Beijing-friendly incumbent and his pro-Washington challenger.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who maintains close ties with Beijing, is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term.
His rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro – son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who was jailed last year for attempting a military coup – was confirmed on Saturday as the Liberal Party’s candidate to challenge Lula in October’s election. His father has been sentenced to more than 27 years in prison over the coup plot, but is now under house arrest due to health issues.
Analysts warn that a victory for the opposition senator could mean an “automatic alignment” with Washington, while pragmatic ties with Beijing are likely to endure because of close commercial relations.
Days after the US Trade Representative’s office imposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff under Section 301 on major trading partners, including China and Brazil, Chinese President Xi Jinping told Lula that Beijing was ready to support Brazil in “safeguarding its own sovereignty and independence, and opposing foreign interference”.
In the phone call on Monday at Lula’s request, Xi said Beijing attached great importance to Brazil’s international status and significant influence.

title: Why use rare earths in rubber production? Chinese scientists are engineering tougher tyres
summary:
Chinese researchers have completed trials of a new rare earth-based synthetic rubber production facility, industrialising a major raw material for manufacturing electric vehicle and heavy-duty vehicle tyres.
High-quality synthetic rubber, most of which uses metal as a catalyst during production, is vital to the transport industry, manufacturing and national defence.
The unit, built by Xinjiang-based PetroChina subsidiary Dushanzi Petrochemical with support from the Changchun Institute of Applied...
full_text:
Why use rare earths in rubber production? Chinese scientists are engineering tougher tyres
A new facility leverages decades of research to produce high-strength rubber designed to meet requirements of EVs and heavy-duty transport
Starting production on July 16, the plant draws on more than 60 years of research into rare earth catalytic synthesis of butadiene rubber, which the institute said it helped to pioneer in the 1960s.
Butadiene rubber is a type of synthetic rubber that is highly resilient and wear-resistant, and is used to produce tyres and other high-quality rubber-based products. Cis-butadiene rubber refers to a high-grade form engineered to have better durability and elasticity.
Butadiene rubber is typically produced using a metal-based catalyst, mainly nickel, titanium, cobalt, or rare earth metals. One of the main catalytic systems uses neodymium, a rare earth metal produced mainly by China.

full_text:
South Asia is undergoing a gradual but important shift. Smaller states now command a widening array of options, and India’s primacy is quietly giving way. The lesson is clear. Regional leadership can no longer rest on geography and must be sustained through credible and mutually beneficial engagements that compare favourably with the alternatives.
China’s challenge begins at India’s border. Both countries 
fought in 1962, continue to dispute a frontier of roughly 3,500km and had their deadliest confrontation in decades in the 
Galwan Valley in 2020. Relations have 
cautiously normalised but the underlying strategic rivalry remains unresolved.
Economic dependence complicates the rivalry. India imported nearly US$132 billion of Chinese goods in the year ended March, more than from any other country. A government analysis has since reportedly identified about US$51 billion in critical imports that could be replaced by pushing domestic production, partly to reduce reliance on China. Thus, China competes strategically with India while retaining considerable influence over its industrial supply chains.
Pakistan provides the clearest expression of Beijing’s regional strategy. China supplied 
81 per cent of Pakistan’s major arms imports between 2020 and 2024. This year, Pakistan commissioned the first of eight Chinese-designed 
Hangor-class submarines under a US$5 billion programme. It also 
raised 1.75 billion yuan (US$258 million) through its first yuan-denominated sovereign “panda bond” in China’s market.
Bangladesh, meanwhile, illustrates the risks of tying bilateral relations too closely to one political party. India’s partnership with former prime minister Sheikh Hasina strengthened bilateral cooperation but 
her fall – her government was deposed after a popular movement in 2024 and her party, the 
Awami League, banned – exposed the weakness of that approach. Her continued 
stay in New Delhi does not help India’s relationship with Bangladesh. Consequently, China’s influence is expected to expand.
New Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s decision to 
include China in his first overseas tour carried political weight. In Beijing last month, he met Chinese President Xi Jinping and sought greater cooperation and investment. The visit showed Bangladesh can use its growing ties with China to negotiate with India from a 
stronger position.

title: Secret tape recordings and ‘sham’ payments: the Liberals’ internal ideological war laid bare
summary:
The NSW anti-corruption watchdog has begun a public inquiry into allegations of branch stacking, illegal donations, and interference with preselections

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

If you ever thought branch stacking was a harmless game played by young, ambitious political operatives seeking to advance within the party, think again.

On Monday, on the first day of the corruption watchdog’s inquiry into operation Rosny, an investigation into allegations of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”, we heard boasts on secret tape recordings from a developer that he had “my hands on the state government” and he had “fucked” the career of a state politician by “taking his seat”. As for the state’s building commissioner, David Chandler, who was a thorn in the developer’s side, he was going to “fuck him sideways”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
If you ever thought branch stacking was a harmless game played by young, ambitious political operatives seeking to advance within the party, think again.
On Monday, on the first day of the corruption watchdog’s inquiry into operation Rosny, an investigation into allegations of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”, we heard boasts on secret tape recordings from a developer that he had “my hands on the state government” and he had “fucked” the career of a state politician by “taking his seat”. As for the state’s building commissioner, David Chandler, who was a thorn in the developer’s side, he was going to “fuck him sideways”.
In another call, in September 2021, the developer, Jean Nassif, reflects on the “fucking bitch”, the then premier Gladys Berejiklian. “Mate, we thought we’re gonna change her,” he says to the other person on the call, Charles Perrottet.
The opening address of counsel assisting the New South Wales Independent Commission of Inquiry, Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC laid out the allegations in horrifying detail. She said that Nassif, now a fugitive in Lebanon, had used his millions to engage the services of a group of Liberal operatives, known as the Reformers, as consultants.
These young men, Dwyer alleges, ran a major branch stacking operation that was designed to take over the Liberal party and promote their conservative agenda, while at the same time using their influence to deliver the outcomes their benefactor sought.
It was not just idle boasting by Nassif. Soon after that taped call, he got what he wanted: the Baulkham Hills MP, David Elliott, lost his preselection. Kevin Anderson, the minister responsible for the building commissioner, was replaced and Chandler, under enormous pressure, resigned.
The Reformers, Icac heard, included two of the former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet’s brothers – Jean-Claude and Charles – as well as the principals of two public relations firms, Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood.
Dwyer alleges Ellis and Greenwood took consultancy payments over a period of three years between 2019 and 2022, from Nassif and others.
These were “sham” payments, she says, and no real work was provided for these payments.
Instead the money was, she alleges, an illegal donation to the Reformers, and the consultancies an elaborate scheme to avoid either caps on the amount of donations or to funnel donations from banned donors – such as developers and those from the liquor and gaming industry – or both.
The alleged amounts are staggering: $2m from Nassif, more than $250,000 from the Catholic Schools Association and $125,000 from lawyer turned publican Michael O’Hara, who also happens to be the former law partner of right-wing Liberal powerbroker and upper house MP, Damien Tudehope. Tudehope stood down from the frontbench after being called as a witness to the inquiry.
Dwyer also gave hints of the evidence the Icac might have: a huge trove of “encrypted messages” between the young men who are central to this investigation. It appears they are now decrypted.
Icac also has evidence of the fundraisers the Reformers held, at which high-profile members of the Liberal party and others, including Tudehope, Tony Abbott and Alan Jones, were speakers.
Dwyer stressed that what she has outlined are at this stage allegations, not evidence, and that it was for the Icac commissioner, Fabian Gleeson SC, to decide the nature of the payments and crucially, the intentions of the key actors.
She urged the public not to get despondent at the sheer scale and breadth of the alleged schemes.
But it will be hard for those who follow this inquiry not to feel very alarmed about the state of our democracy, and what it may imply about how both major parties select candidates and determine policy and priorities.
For the first time we are seeing the internal ideological war within the Liberal party laid bare.
Dwyer read from a dossier – the Reformers’ sales pitch- which was prepared to recruit donors and members.
It says they planned to recruit 5,000 members by 2022 and take back the NSW Liberal party for conservatives, aimed to deliver 75% of the seats in the NSW parliament to conservatives by 2023, and sought control over the Liberal party’s peak body, the NSW state executive.
Their agenda? More conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.
But branch stacking requires significant funds, both to pay the fees of the members who are stacked and the time of the stackers. They needed cash – and that meant finding covert donations.
“Money in politics as in other spheres has the potential to corrupt,” Dwyer told the inquiry.
Just how she alleges it corrupted in NSW remains to be seen. But her opening address hinted that it may have infected decisions on developments, Liberal party preselections, and led to attempts to unseat the building commissioner, David Chandler, to name a few.
Before the ALP gets too smug about the tsunami of horrible news that is going to engulf the NSW Liberals, there is a third allegation of blackmail and corrupt conduct involving Labor councillors at Strathfield council.
They appear to have caught, on the phone taps uncovered during operation Rosny, allegedly planning blackmail of a fellow councillor.
For all major political parties facing an ascendant One Nation, who markets itself as anti-establishment, this inquiry could not have come at a worse time.
Trust in our major parties is low. It’s about to get much lower.

title: Pauline Hanson and Malcolm Roberts deride family law system, calling DV a ‘weapon’ and court a ‘slaughterhouse’
summary:
Exclusive: Resurfaced comments by the One Nation leader underline her criticism of paid family violence leave and domestic violence support groups

Pauline Hanson told a podcast last year she believed “your employer should not be responsible” for providing paid domestic violence leave, while her colleague Malcolm Roberts recently referred to the family court as the “slaughterhouse of the nation”, in the latest One Nation comments critical of the family law system to emerge.

Hanson claimed on a 2021 podcast that domestic violence was being “used as a weapon” in court proceedings, and criticised domestic violence groups for focusing on support for women.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Pauline Hanson told a podcast last year she believed “your employer should not be responsible” for providing paid domestic violence leave, while her colleague Malcolm Roberts recently referred to the family court as the “slaughterhouse of the nation”, in the latest One Nation comments critical of the family law system to emerge.
Hanson claimed on a 2021 podcast that domestic violence was being “used as a weapon” in court proceedings, and criticised domestic violence groups for focusing on support for women.
“I feel for the children, I feel for the parents and I’m sick of these feminists who are trying to take over this whole thing and who are actually driving their own agenda. I’m sick and tired of hearing that men are the only perpetrators and they’re denied the right to see their children,” Hanson told the Dad Talk Today podcast in 2021.
Hanson’s past comments on domestic violence have drawn renewed scrutiny after a 4BC radio interview last week in which she said family violence was “wrong” but “it’s also a two-way street”.
In an interview with the Broken Fathers podcast last year, Hanson described paid leave for those experiencing family and domestic violence as “ridiculous”, calling it “domestic violence holiday leave”. She also suggested domestic violence was taking police away from “real crime” and called for the family law system to be “wound back”.
Hanson later claimed her 4BC comments had been taken “out of context” and denied she had downplayed domestic violence.
But the newly unearthed comments show the full breadth of One Nation’s criticism of the family law system.
In an interview with Hanson for a podcast titled Unemployable Media in January 2025, during a discussion about challenges facing business owners, the podcast host brought up the issue of domestic violence leave.
“Nobody in Australia would say domestic violence isn’t a horrible thing, but you’ve got 10 days,” the host began saying, before Hanson interjected.
“It should not be tied up in your employment. Your employer should not be responsible,” Hanson said.
The federal Labor government in 2022 legislated for 10 days of paid family and domestic violence leave annually as a workplace entitlement in the National Employment Standards, upgrading the previous five days’ unpaid leave. The cost is borne by employers.
Some businesses raised concerns when the change was legislated, but the social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said only “a tiny number of people” used the leave.
“But they use it to get medical help, report to police, move to a safer home or go to court”.
The ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, said the scheme was “an essential lifeline available to workers facing some horrifically dangerous situations”.
In the 2021 interview, the One Nation leader criticised “feminist” groups in the domestic violence system.
“You have the domestic violence organisations, they’re getting millions of dollars in funding for it. You’ve got these refuges – and I can see that a woman needs to be protected if they don’t have a house to actually go to with the kids, a safe place to go … but you’ve got to offer the same to a man. You can’t just look after women,” Hanson said.
Later in the interview Hanson claimed domestic violence was “used as a weapon” in court.
“Domestic violence here is, the person can go in and say ‘I’m in fear’ and that can be domestic violence. If you text your partner a number of times ‘I want to see my child’, that’s harassment, that can be domestic violence. If you say ‘honey, sorry why’d you buy another pair of shoes? We’ve got the rent to pay’, that’s domestic violence.”
Roberts, whose advocacy of conspiracy theories has come under scrutiny, also criticised the family court system in a May interview with the rightwing podcast Cafe Locked Out.
“The family law court, a friend of mine describes the family law system as the slaughterhouse of the nation and he’s right,” Roberts said.
“It’s set up to divide. It’s set up to make money for lawyers. It’s set up to smash the family.”
One Nation and Hanson’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Potential for first Australian oil refinery in 60 years as treasurer braces for inflation from Middle East war
summary:
Commonwealth and Western Australia to fund study into construction of large-scale petrol refinery as buffer against fuel vulnerability

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s first new oil refinery in 60 years could be built in Western Australia under the Albanese government’s long-term strategy to shield the country from future global oil shocks.

The commonwealth and the WA government will fund a $4m early-stage feasibility study into construction of what would be the country’s third large-scale petrol refinery.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Australia’s first new oil refinery in 60 years could be built in Western Australia under the Albanese government’s long-term strategy to shield the country from future global oil shocks.
The commonwealth and the WA government will fund a $4m early-stage feasibility study into construction of what would be the country’s third large-scale petrol refinery.
A series of refinery closures over the past 25 years means Australia now imports about 90% of its liquid fuels, a vulnerability exposed by the international oil crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The announcement comes as Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, warned the recent escalation of the Middle East conflict posed “a substantial threat to global inflation”.
Treasury officials in a special weekend government briefing warned the collapse of the ceasefire meant oil prices were likely to remain high in the near future.
“The oil market is now more vulnerable, with weaker buffers against future supply shocks,” the officials said.
With petrol and diesel prices up by 25 cents and 50 cents a litre this month, respectively, the rekindling of the conflict has also boosted expectations that central banks will need to do more to bring inflation back under control – piling more pressure on households.
“The longer this drags out the more serious the consequences for inflation and growth here and around the world,” Chalmers said.
Financial markets were pricing a one-in-three chance of a Reserve Bank rate hike on 11 August. That was down from an even chance on Friday after Brent crude, the oil benchmark, tumbled more than US$10 a barrel on Monday to about US$87 after a pause in fighting over the weekend.
Australia’s oil refining industry has struggled to compete with cheaper overseas providers.
There are just two local refineries in operation: Ampol’s Lytton refinery in Brisbane and Viva Energy’s facility in Geelong.
Building a new refinery would cost billions of dollars, and would probably require ongoing government support to stay competitive.
The proposed WA project, were it to go ahead, would be constructed by Perdaman, the large multinational behind a $4.5bn fertiliser plant in the Pilbara. Perdaman would privately fund the project but could be eligible for taxpayer-funded assistance, such as concessional loans.
BP closed an oil refinery in Fremantle, just south of Perth, in 2021.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and WA premier, Roger Cook, will announce funding for the scoping study after visiting Perdaman’s urea plant in Karratha.
“The longer war in the Middle East goes on the greater the impact on Australia will be, and my government will continue to do everything we can to shield Australia from the worst effects – and set us up for the future,” Albanese said in a statement.
The federal government’s $10.7bn fuel security package, announced in May, included $10m to support feasibility studies into potential projects.
The package also funded a $7.5bn facility to secure extra fuel and fertiliser shipments during the Middle East conflict, and $3.2bn to build an extra 1 billion-litre reserve of diesel and jet fuel.
Chris Bowen, the energy minister, described plans to boost domestic refining capacity as “a sensible and prudent response to secure our energy security”.
But the early-stage support for a new oil refinery will probably face push-back from environmentalists, who have criticised the federal government for doubling down on petrol and diesel rather than using the oil shock to reduce Australia’s reliance on fossil fuels.

title: ‘I knew what he had done to those boys’: murderer to stay in jail after journalist’s fight for justice
summary:
Gibraltar-based Ros Astengo inspired four men to report sexual assaults carried out by Allan Grimson in 1990s

Ros Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.

She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Ros Astengo, a journalist based in Gibraltar who usually focuses on politics and social issues, had qualms when she began investigating the case of the suspected serial killer Allan Grimson as he neared release from prison after serving more than 20 years.
She worried that she might reopen the scars of survivors of Grimson – but also that she could be putting herself in the “crosshairs” of a dangerous man who had sexually assaulted and battered two young men to death in the late 1990s when he was a Royal Navy petty officer.
“But the public interest overrode it,” Astengo said. “It would have been so easy for me to have just done nothing. But I thought to myself, how would I feel if as soon as they let him out he reoffended and harmed another young man. My motive was to keep the public safe.”
Because of Astengo’s work, four men came forward to report sexual assaults by Grimson carried out on them in the same era as the two murders.
On Monday, a jury at Winchester crown court found Grimson guilty of 13 sexual offences relating to the men, which may mean he remains in prison for years to come.
Judge Dugdale told Grimson he was an extremely dangerous man in the 1990s and asked for reports to be prepared to help him understand if he still posed a serious risk.
The judge also asked for victim personal statements to be taken from the men. He thanked the jury for hearing a “very unusual case” and invited them to return to court when he sentenced Grimson in November.
“The men were incredibly brave to come to court, bring all this back into their lives,” Astengo said.
Grimson was jailed for life in 2001 and told he would serve at least 22 years in prison for sexually abusing and murdering Nicholas Wright, 18, and Sion Jenkins, 20, in Portsmouth, both of whom had served in the navy. The sentencing judge described him as a “serial killer in nature if not by number”.
At the time, Grimson also admitted in police interviews sexual offences or contact with another four men – three young sailors and a teenage boy. He said he had thought of killing two of them but the Crown Prosecution Service did not pursue the allegations because he was going to serve a long jail term for the murders anyway.
While in prison Grimson was on best behaviour in the hope that he would be released after serving his 22 years and in November 2020 the Parole Board recommended he be moved to an open prison to prepare him for freedom.
At this time, Astengo was covering the search for the body of another sailor, Simon Parkes, who vanished in Gibraltar in 1986. Grimson was in the British overseas territory at the time. He has long been a suspect but denies involvement.
No remains were found and Astengo said she was deeply moved when Parkes’s elderly parents, Margaret and David, from south-west England, described it as their last chance to get justice. “It was a very lonely journey for them.” She promised them she would write a book about their son’s case to keep his memory alive.
She began her research and was disturbed to find he had made admissions over the four boys and young men but no action had been taken.
“I was astonished that he was never charged over them,” Astengo said. She was alarmed that Grimson seemed close to being released. “I knew what he had done to those boys. That really worried me. How could he be fully rehabilitated? I was worried he would go back into the community thinking he’s gotten away with it. I realised I was putting myself in the crosshairs of a killer but I thought something needed to be done.”
Astengo tracked down one of the four and travelled to the UK to speak to him. “I found a very angry man who was still hurt, angry and upset that he had never seen justice. He started talking about the fact that he was older now and a parent. He understands today what he didn’t back then – that was that he was groomed.”
Astengo told the man he could file a fresh complaint about Grimson. “I said to him, think very carefully about what you’re doing because you are going to open a can of worms for yourself.”
The man went ahead and spoke to police. Initially no action was taken so Astengo contacted the child sexual abuse review panel, which examines allegations of non-recent child sexual offences.
It agreed that the case was worth re-examining. Detectives interviewed the man and tracked down the three others. In February 2025, Grimson was charged over the attacks on the four.
The month-long trial highlighted how far the justice system had come in dealing with sexual crimes.
In the late 1990s and early 2000s it was not uncommon for serious sexual allegations not to be pursued if a defendant faced a long jail sentence for even more serious crimes. Now it is considered the state’s duty to do so.
It is also a reminder that until the turn of the century, gay people were not allowed to serve openly in the armed forces, meaning some of those assaulted by Grimson were keen not to talk about what had happened back then because they feared dismissal.
In court, Grimson’s legal team tried to argue that it was unfair for him to be charged with offences that the authorities had not pursued a quarter of a century ago. They made it clear he felt he was being prosecuted now as a tactic for keeping him in prison, to “stymie” his parole.
His legal team also criticised Astengo, suggesting she had been motivated by making money from her book, which is due to come out next year.
John Price KC, prosecuting, urged the jury to ignore “conspiracy theories” about Astengo’s involvement and said good was achieved by energetic journalists.
Astengo said it was not about money. Every time she travelled to the UK she has had to pay her own way, take leave – and could make very little, if anything, from her book. She said: “The defence tried to paint me as somebody who has exerted undue influence all because I’m writing a book. For me, it was about justice and to prevent a serial offender from being released.”

title: Mayo beat 75-year-old ‘curse’ to become Gaelic football champions
summary:

The hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitched Ireland for decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.

Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team to endless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.

full_text:
The hex is broken, dispelled, banished, and a story that bewitched Ireland for decades has ended in fairytale: Mayo are all-Ireland champions.
Seventy-five years after a supposed curse condemned its Gaelic men’s football team to endless defeat, the county prevailed and uncorked a wave of emotion that engulfed even its rivals.
The team will return to the west of Ireland for a euphoric homecoming on Monday evening after winning the senior football championship, a victory that thrilled Ireland and Mayo’s diaspora, including Joe Biden, Mark Carney and Noel and Liam Gallagher.
“Mayo 1-20, Kerry 1-17. Chisel it on the gravestones, scribble it in the sky,” the Irish Times exulted. “Croke Park untethered, the whole place afloat for an hour on a lake of the sweetest tears that were ever cried.”
Most pundits had favoured Kerry to win the 138th all-Ireland final and write another chapter of Mayo woe at Sunday’s contest at the Dublin stadium. Instead the underdogs triumphed and even some Kerry fans wept at the catharsis.
Few seriously believed in the curse – it was said no member of the last winning team from 1951 would live to see another – but there was no doubting the drought that followed, with 11 defeats in 11 finals since 1989. A book about Mayo’s quest was titled House of Pain.
Whenever the county made it to a final, a frisson gripped television viewers and the 82,000-strong stadium crowd: was this the day they would witness the end of the hex? On Sunday it was.
“To every young boy and girl across Mayo and our diaspora across the world, never stop dreaming, stick your chest out and be proud to be from Mayo,” the team captain, Jack Coyne, declared as he held aloft the trophy named after Sam Maguire, a legendary player. “The wait is over. Sam is home.”
Authorities had provisionally estimated a crowd of 40,000 would greet the team at McHale Park in the county town of Castlebar on Monday but that looks conservative, Gerry Bourke, the homecoming committee chair, told RTÉ. “After what I saw in Croke Park yesterday, I think we’ll have to revisit the plan.”
Mayo, a landscape of bogs, rocks and Atlantic cliffs, is the third biggest of the island of Ireland’s 32 counties. It is sparsely populated, with just 130,000 people, but players and supporters have a reputation for fervency in the Gaelic Athletic Association, the sport’s governing body.
According to lore, the young victors of 1951 were on their way home to celebrate when they passed through the village of Foxford and failed to pay their respects to a funeral, prompting the enraged priest to utter the fateful words: “For as long as you all live, Mayo won’t win another all-Ireland.”
Seven decades later, the last surviving member of that team, Paddy Prendergast, told friends he would willingly “roll over and die” if there was any truth to the curse, but that it was a myth.
“There was supposed to have been a funeral in the local church; I don’t know whether there was or not. I saw people standing around the church but we didn’t get off the truck because we couldn’t get off the bloody truck,” he told an interviewer in 2017.
Researchers who probed church records, press cuttings and other sources failed to find any verification of the supposed curse, which gained currency in the 1990s. The legend, however, is intact: Prendergast died in 2021, aged 95, two weeks after Mayo lost the final.
Biden – who concluded a 2023 presidential visit to Mayo with the rallying cry “Mayo for Sam!” – congratulated his ancestral home county. “Today, the dream becomes reality,” he posted. “You earned this victory. Enjoy every minute.”
Carney, the Canadian prime minister who made his own ancestral pilgrimage to Mayo last month, echoed the joy. “The curse is broken,” he posted. The Gallagher brothers of Oasis, who also have family ties to Mayo, expressed pride. “Finally!! Up Mayo!!” Noel posted.

title: German officials call for tighter extremism laws after Berlin Pride attack
summary:
Alternative für Deutschland, topping polls ahead of state elections, accuses government of failing to tackle Islamist radicalism

  • Europe live – latest updates

German officials have called for a tightening of laws for known extremists after a deadly attack in Berlin on one of Europe’s biggest Pride parades, as the far right seeks to mobilise outraged voters before three key state elections.

The anti-migration, anti-Islam Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the top party in national opinion polls, accused the government of failing to tackle Islamist radicalism on German soil, while the conservative chancellor, Friedrich Merz, pledged to act with “prudence but also determination” to address security gaps.

Continue reading...
full_text:
German officials have called for a tightening of laws for known extremists after a deadly attack in Berlin on one of Europe’s biggest Pride parades, as the far right seeks to mobilise outraged voters before three key state elections.
The anti-migration, anti-Islam Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the top party in national opinion polls, accused the government of failing to tackle Islamist radicalism on German soil, while the conservative chancellor, Friedrich Merz, pledged to act with “prudence but also determination” to address security gaps.
Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German national with Lebanese roots who was well known to police, is believed to have rammed a van into a crowd in Tiergarten park late on Saturday, next to the finale of annual LGBTQ+ celebrations that drew hundreds of thousands of people.
After the vehicle, which had been rented in Ballout’s name, crashed into a tree, he allegedly attacked people with a large knife. A 65-year-old Polish woman died and 29 others were injured.
Following an hours-long manhunt, police said they shot Ballout dead in a garden allotment in the Spandau district on Sunday after he ran at them with a “bladed weapon” when they attempted to arrest him.
Merz said on Monday the victims had been rallying for “openness, diversity and freedom”, and were assaulted by “an Islamist who sought to attack those values”.
As thousands gathered for a sombre ceremony at the Brandenburg Gate in central Berlin to mourn the victims, it emerged police had been aware of the risk posed by Ballout as an avowed Islamic extremist with previous arrests for bodily harm, extortion and robbery.
Security authorities said Ballout was a supporter of Islamic State and last year attempted to join the group in Syria. He was arrested in Lebanon and repatriated, and in May was convicted in Germany of “preparing a serious act of subversive violence”.
Berlin-born Ballout, who lived with his divorced mother and two sisters in the capital, was sentenced as a juvenile to a year and 10 months in prison. But the Berlin court suspended the sentence and he was allowed to walk free, albeit under sporadic police observation.
Berlin’s top justice official, Felor Badenberg, on Monday acknowledged public anger over the case after a deadly series of car ramming and knife attacks in Germany, and urged an overhaul of juvenile criminal law.
“In the wake of this attack, my conclusion is that, in cases such as this, the perpetrators must indeed be punished more severely,” Badenberg, a member of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told public broadcaster ARD.
While acknowledging the courts’ independence, she said: “We must fundamentally examine whether the legal criteria we currently have for applying juvenile criminal law are still appropriate for the times.”
Berlin, one of Germany’s federal states, will go to the polls in September along with two other eastern regions. In all three elections, the far-right AfD is expected to perform well, and is poised to take first place in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
The AfD, founded 13 years ago as a Eurosceptic movement, has seized on fears around immigration and crime and more recently zeroed in on economic woes linked to German deindustrialisation, allowing it to make inroads beyond its eastern heartland.
Party co-leader Alice Weidel accused Merz on Monday of failing to take the problem of Islamist extremism and “migrant violence” seriously.
“Merz remains silent on Islamism – we are ready to take action!” she posted on X.
The AfD’s main candidate for the Berlin election, Kristin Brinker, blamed the Pride attack on the “catastrophic migration policy of the last few years”.
Experts said the AfD could stand to gain from the tragedy. The party is already polling at between 38 and 40% in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, within striking distance of an absolute majority for the first time at the state level.
Guido Friebel, dean of the economics faculty at Goethe University in Frankfurt, has conducted research with a team of colleagues on how terrorist attacks affect the AfD’s electoral outcomes.
“The AfD has made [the interplay between] migration and internal security one of its key issues,” he told Der Spiegel magazine. “It will capitalise politically on this attack.”
Friebel said the AfD even benefited at the polls from attacks carried out by rightwing extremists, creating a dilemma for mainstream democratic parties such as the CDU, which have sought to establish a law-and-order profile.
“If it [the CDU] ignores the issue, the AfD can claim that it is the only party taking the threat seriously,” he said. “If it adopts their issues and rhetoric, there is a risk that it will contribute to strengthening the AfD’s political agenda.”
Counter-extremism expert Hans-Jakob Schindler, who advises the German government, told local media there were more than 9,000 Islamists living in the country in 2025, including 2,590 in the capital, 1,940 of whom are believed to be violent.
The LSVD+ queer advocacy group said homophobic and anti-trans attacks had increased tenfold in Germany in recent years.
With several LGBTQ+ marches still to come this summer including in Hamburg, Nuremberg and Dortmund, community activists said they had been sounding the alarm about a rising threat from Islamists as well as far-right extremists, but were not being heard.
“Now we see that comes at a price,” said Alva Träbert, an LSVD+ board member.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Boy George has released a new song entitled We Will Dance Again, which voices support for Israel’s military action in Palestine.
Posted on X and Instagram with the Hebrew title עוד נרקוד alongside its English translation, the song features a pop-reggae backing. The opening lyrics are: “You say genocide, I say war / When you’re attacked, that’s what the army’s for / Does it get ugly? You bet it does / When I know you wanna kill every last one of us.”
Boy George cites the attack by Hamas at the Nova music festival in October 2023, saying the civilians killed there were “murder[ed] … for the crime of dancing”. A total of 344 civilians and 34 security personnel were killed and 44 people were taken hostage.
The overall Palestinian death toll since the war started is more than 73,000.
The title phrase We Will Dance Again, repeated for the song’s chorus, has been used by Israelis to express hope and solidarity in the wake of the 7 October attack, and was used as the title of an acclaimed documentary about it.
Elsewhere in the chorus, Boy George asserts: “There will be no war / But if you’re ever confused / I stand with the Jews / I don’t feel brave, I just need to behave like a human.”
He also criticises the pro-Palestinian movement, including musicians who have condemned Israel: “You condemn the Jews, with selective memory / Musicians holding flags, mouthing like sheep / Propaganda fuelled by the internet feels so weak.” Musicians who have supported Palestine include Stormzy, Damon Albarn, Clairo and Brian Eno, the latter of whom conceived an all-star charity single, Lullaby, which vied for Christmas No 1 in 2025.
Boy George, who is not Jewish, has recently voiced support for Jewish communities. In an interview with the Telegraph, when discussing his admiration for Jewish peers in the 1980s during his time fronting Culture Club, he said: “Over the years it’s been a really personal thing. It doesn’t mean that I don’t have compassion for Palestinians, it doesn’t mean that I agree with what’s going on in Israel, but I am always going to defend the people that I love. I have a lot of Jewish friends and there would never be a situation where I’d turn my back on them.”
He also voiced his support after the knife attack in Golders Green in April which left two Jewish men injured, saying: “We need to make our Jewish community know we support them.”
His new song marks an intensification of his support for Israel, having said earlier in the year that he didn’t have an opinion on the country.
Speaking ahead of an appearance with San Marino for their Eurovision song contest entry (which didn’t reach the contest’s final), he was questioned about the boycott of Eurovision from countries opposing Israel’s inclusion in the contest. “I have many Jewish friends, whom I’ve known since I was 15 or 16 years old,” he replied. “Are people asking me, as someone with principles, to turn my back on my Jewish friends? That is not going to happen – it will never happen. From the beginning of my career, I wore the Star of David … I feel very connected to the Jewish people. I’m not necessarily connected to Israel. I don’t really have an opinion on that. But the mission of music is to unite people.”
His characterisation of Israel’s action against Palestine as a legitimate military response rather than genocide runs counter to a United Nations inquiry, which stated in 2025 that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel’s foreign ministry called the report “distorted and false”. Last month, another independent UN inquiry found that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by targeting children. That report was dubbed a “libellous sham” by Israel.
Boy George was one of the most flamboyant and recognisable pop stars of the 1980s, with Culture Club scoring four UK Top 10 albums including 1983’s chart-topping Colour By Numbers. Hit singles include Do You Really Want to Hurt Me? and Karma Chameleon, which were both hugely successful in the US as well as UK, and have endured as staples on oldies radio.
The band also had a hit with an anti-war track, The War Song, which reached UK No 2 in 1984 and featured the chorus: “War is stupid and people are stupid / And love means nothing in some strange quarters.”
Last month, Boy George launched a new company called Artist Included, which will use AI to allow artists to create new versions of earlier songs which resemble the originals, as a way of wresting back control of master recordings. It launched with a new version of Karma Chameleon, which Boy George recorded then de-aged. “When I heard it, I was absolutely gobsmacked,” he told the Hollywood Reporter. “It sounds like another take from that original session.”

title: 15 Habits Infectious Disease Experts Swear By to Avoid Getting Sick
summary: They follow surprisingly simple rules to prevent illness.
full_text:
Dr. Daniel Griffin doesn’t like to get sick. The first reason why is obvious—the congestion, the aching, the cough that overstays its welcome, the unpleasant stomach symptoms.
The second is a matter of professional dignity. "It's almost like a gardener with dead plants," says Griffin, chief of the division of infectious disease at Island Infectious Disease Medical in Long Island, N.Y. and president of Parasites Without Borders. "I really don't want to be sick—because then the infectious disease doctor got sick.”
So what do infectious disease doctors and experts like him do differently than the rest of us when it comes to preventing illness? Not as much as you'd think. Infectious disease specialists aren't disinfecting every surface or hiding from the outside world. Instead, they've built a collection of practical habits into their daily lives—simple routines that reduce risk without making life less enjoyable.
We asked six infectious disease experts which habits they never skip.
Set up your kitchen so cross-contamination can't happen
Jill Roberts tries to take the guesswork out of food safety. "One of the major causes of foodborne illness is cross-contamination," says Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health. "It's when you have something that's raw and you get microbes from the raw thing into the ready-to-eat thing."
Her favorite solution: color-coded cutting boards. Meat always goes on the red one; vegetables never do. "If your meat is always on the red cutting board, you're never gonna have your salad stuff on your red cutting board,” she says.
Order matters just as much. She makes the salad first, puts it in the refrigerator, and only then brings out the red boards and raw meat. Once she starts handling meat, she’s vigilant about sanitizing any surfaces she may have contaminated—from the counters and sink to the faucet handles and refrigerator door.
Wash your produce under running water—not in a bowl
Some people think rinsing produce means filling a bowl with water and letting everything soak. But that's not the best approach. "What you actually need is that little bit of friction to break the surface," says Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious disease physician and assistant professor of clinical medicine at Weill Cornell Medical College. About 30 seconds under running water, while gently rubbing the produce with your hands, does far more than a passive soak.
The problem with a bowl is that you're washing everything in the same water. "If you have one piece that's contaminated, that water could contaminate the other vegetables," Torres says. Running water washes germs away instead of moving them from one piece of produce to another. It won't remove everything—Cyclospora, for example, doesn't simply rinse off—but it does reduce bacteria, viruses, and even some pesticide residue.
Microwave your kitchen sponge
A sponge is a nearly perfect habitat for germs: damp, warm, and studded with food particles, sitting next to the counter where you just set down raw chicken. "Sponges and wet dishcloths are really good at growing bacteria," says Kelley Steury, a clinical associate professor in the school of public health at the University of Nevada, Reno, who specializes in veterinary preventive medicine. Her routine: Rinse her sponge until no food particles come out, then microwave it for 20 seconds. Just make sure it's wet. "If you did it when it was pretty dry, you could start a fire,” she says.
Brush your teeth like it's infection control
Most people brush their teeth to prevent cavities. Torres brushes hers to prevent infections.
"At least 25% of infections that I see are related to dental disease," she says. Here's why: Every day, small amounts of bacteria slip into your bloodstream, and a healthy immune system clears them without you ever noticing. Cavities and gum disease change the equation. They allow more bacteria—and more aggressive bacteria—to leak into the blood, which Torres describes as "a highway to all your organs." In some cases, she says, doctors can trace an infection back to the mouth because the bacteria involved simply don't live anywhere else.
That makes brushing about much more than fresh breath. "Rinsing alone wouldn’t replace it, because you really need that mechanical brushing to break down that film of bacteria," Torres says. Hospitals have even started treating basic oral care as a form of infection prevention, she says—which is a pretty compelling reason to take it seriously at home, too.
Rethink the rug in your bathroom
Your bath mat outside the tub should be washable, hung to dry between uses, and tossed in the laundry about once a week. "We don't leave the wet stuff on the floor, because that's gross," Roberts says. A damp bath mat can also spread athlete's foot from one person to another.
As for the old-fashioned rug wrapped around the base of the toilet? Roberts would get rid of it altogether. Rubber backings don’t often hold up well in the wash, which means it probably doesn't get cleaned as thoroughly as it should. "Especially if you have kids, they don't aim well," she says. "You have splash-overs." In other words: Nothing around the toilet should be soaking anything up.
Leave your shoes at the door
Shoes pick up a lot more than dirt. Every sidewalk has been shared with other people, their pets, and whatever else has passed through. Dr. Cesar J. Figueroa Ortiz, an infectious diseases specialist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, would rather not track any of that across the floors where his family walks and spends time—so shoes come off at the door.
His job reinforces the habit. Hospitals are meticulously cleaned, but there's always "the risk of bringing pathogens with you on your shoes," he says.
Open a window before company comes over
Before guests arrive, most people wipe down the counters. Chin-Hong thinks they should be paying more attention to the air. "I respect air more than surfaces," he says. "You're probably going to have a bigger bang for your buck when you think about ventilation."
His solution is simple: crack a window. If the air conditioning is running, make sure it's bringing in fresh outdoor air rather than recirculating the same indoor air all evening, he adds.
Wash your hands like you're not in a hurry
Even infectious disease doctors don't always practice perfect hand hygiene. Griffin has watched colleagues race out of a public restroom because they were about to miss a lecture at a conference. "They're so anxious to get back out because they're missing whatever the lecture is, and they're not really doing proper hand hygiene," he says. "Even the people that should know better are rushing back out."
And when people do wash their hands, they're often rushing through that, too. "Nobody's singing 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' to time themselves," Griffin says (besides him).
His other rule is knowing when soap and water beat sanitizer. (Basically always.) Alcohol-based hand sanitizer doesn't kill everything: Norovirus—the highly contagious stomach bug behind many cruise ship outbreaks—is particularly resistant. Soap and water keep you safe, though, so if someone around you is vomiting or has diarrhea, Griffin says, head for the sink.
Use your shirt tail
Steury will happily look a little strange to save herself a bout with a germ. "Someone might look at me and think I'm crazy, but I'll use the bottom of a shirt, like my shirt tails," she says—or the hem of a cardigan, whatever's handy—around her hand when she has to touch certain surfaces.
She's selective about when she does it. What worries her are high-touch surfaces that are indoors and out of the sun: elevator buttons, soda fountain dispensers, and the door handle to a medical clinic, for instance. And if she does touch one of those surfaces directly, she waits until she can wash her hands before touching her eyes, nose, or mouth.
Decline the grocery-store sample
B
